event.title: Learning Our Inheritance
event.abstract: Every technology carries a legacy. The systems we use today are shaped by decisions, values, and assumptions made long before us. The choices we make now will shape the world that future-generations inherit. Three generations of builders are led through conversation, reflecting on the past, acknowledging the impact on the present, outlining what is needed for our future

Anil Dash (None) / Principle & CoFounder

Anil Dash is a technologist, writer and activist recognized as a leading advocate for making innovative technology that is ethical and inclusive. A Webby Awards lifetime achievement honoree, he has been CEO or founder of several groundbreaking startups including Glitch, the beloved creative community for developers which was acquired by Fastly in 2022. Today, he is principal and cofounder of antitech, which helps organizations thrive by building good, thoughtful technology.

Dash is well-known as a leading voice in the tech industry, uniquely serving as both an analyst of cutting-edge innovations and a critical perspective on the risks and harms that can happen without accountability. As a writer, Dash was a monthly columnist and contributing editor for Wired, and has written for publications ranging from The Atlantic to Rolling Stone to Businessweek, while his venerable personal blog has been cited over the last 25 years by everyone from sitting U.S. Senators to hundreds of academic papers to TMZ.

Today, Dash also serves as a board member for vital social organizations like the Electronic Frontier Foundation, the indispensable nonprofit organization defending digital human rights and free expression, and is chair of the board of the Lower East Side Girls Club, which serves girls and families in need in New York City. Previously, Dash was a technology advisor to the Obama White House's Office of Digital Strategy (and later the Obama Foundation), and served for a decade on the board of Stack Overflow, the world's largest community for coders. Previously, he founded and led a MacArthur-backed research project conducting pioneering research on social media's impact on public policy making. While CEO of Glitch, the company became the first tech startup ever to voluntarily recognize its workers' union.

Described by The New Yorker as a "blogging pioneer", and by the New York Times as a "Prince scholar", he has had a varied career as an artist and creator, co-creating the earliest implementation of the technology later known as NFTs, having his work exhibited in the New Museum of Contemporary Art, and collaborating with Hamilton creator Lin-Manuel Miranda on a wildly popular Spotify playlist serving as an educational throwback mixtape. Back when Twitter was relevant, Time named @anildash one of the best accounts on Twitter. His account remains the only one ever retweeted by both Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and Prince, a succinct summarization of Dash's wide-ranging interests. Dash has also been featured in a broad range of media and stages, ranging from the Aspen Ideas Festival to Desus and Mero's late-night show, and has guested on a surprisingly broad swath of your favorite podcasts.

Dash lives in New York City with his wife Alaina Browne and their child and two dogs. Like most people, he has never played a round of golf, drank a cup of coffee, filed a patent, or graduated from college.

Gitanjali began innovating at a remarkably young age. At just 11, she developed Tethys, a portable technology designed to detect lead contamination in water, inspired by the Flint water crisis. Her work earned her many prestigious awards and recognitions, including Forbes 30 Under 30 in Science.

Her innovations have expanded into healthcare and artificial intelligence. She developed Epione, a proposed early-detection technology for prescription opioid addiction using genetic engineering, and created Kindly, an AI- and natural-language-processing-based platform designed to help identify and combat cyberbullying. Kindly has since been recognized as a UNICEF Digital Public Good and made available globally.

In 2020, Gitanjali became TIME magazine’s first-ever Kid of the Year and was recognized as a TIME Top Young Innovator, following years of innovation, research, and STEM outreach. She was also named a UNICEF Youth Advocate and has used her platform to inspire young people around the world to see themselves as innovators and problem-solvers.

In 2025, Gitanjali became the first recipient of the Stephen Hawking Junior Medal for Science Communication, presented by the Starmus Festival. The honor recognizes her ability to make science accessible and inspire the next generation of scientists and innovators.

Beyond her research and inventions, Gitanjali is a passionate science communicator and educator. Through international workshops and educational initiatives, she has inspired students across dozens of countries. She is also the author of two books designed to help young people develop their own ideas and turn them into meaningful innovations.

Today, Gitanjali continues to pursue research at the forefront of biological engineering, AI, and healthcare innovation, while expanding her mission to make science, technology, and innovation more accessible to young people worldwide.

event.title: Tough Conversations We Need To Have
event.abstract:
AC Coppens guides the room through three pairings between the people building technology and the people living with its consequences. Each pairing examines a specific technological tension through the lived experience of those shaping and experiencing these systems. Rather than seeking easy agreement, AC Coppen’s facilitation creates the conditions for nuanced, honest conversations that reveal the tradeoffs, values, and human consequences embedded in the technologies we build.

Who gets to speak for the dead?

Death used to mean losing someone. AI is making that less certain. AI can now preserve our voices, recreate our likenesses, and keep traces of us present long after death. The same technologies can restore speech, expand accessibility, and reveal intimate information about our bodies and health. But when the data that extends our agency can also outlive our ability to consent, who gets to preserve, analyze, recreate, or profit from what we leave behind. Who gets to speak for the dead?

The Right to Exist, The Right to Disappear

Visibility has become one of technology’s greatest contradictions. Being seen can mean dignity, opportunity, cultural survival, and a voice in systems that have historically excluded you. It can also mean surveillance, extraction, and the loss of control. As technology makes more of us searchable, knowable, and permanent, this conversation asks: who holds the power over when visibility is liberation and when it becomes a violation?

Planted or Transplanted: Sovereignty, Sold Separately

“AI for the Global South” is increasingly built, named, and standardized in the North, then exported as inclusion. Critics warn the very words, sovereignty, regulation, “for good,” are being captured. Yet a billion people gaining real public infrastructure is not nothing. Self-determination, or sovereignty-as-a-service sold by the same hyperscalers it claims to escape? When someone builds your future for your own good, is that care, or is that conquest?

event.title: Crip Intelligence: "Invalid" Parameters for Post-Capitalist Imaginaries of AI
event.abstract:
My performance lecture is designed to arrive at an articulation of Crip Intelligence, as a speculative framework which draws from crip theory to centre "invalid" parameters in the AI pipeline to produce new imaginaries of AI, which has emerged out of my art-pedagogy practice as a disability justice and digital rights actor in the Global South, and more broadly, out of critical disability research and computational histories.

In my work, Crip Intelligence represents an urge, a means, to sabotage and misdirect AI's tendencies of "busily restructuring society — more by dysfunction than by efficiency — contributing to the rise of post-fascist, neofeudal and reactionary movements" (Artificial Stupidity, Hito Steyerl). Throughout the performance-talk, I will be shifting, re-orienting, and maneuvering the language of anti-capitalist affirmations, land acknowledgments, somatic therapy practices and guided meditation, to create the conditions necessary for making new imaginations of AI possible: imaginations that are rooted in small, slow, frugal, esoteric, decolonial, and feminist principles.

I present Crip Intelligence as a speculative strategy that allows me to explore if there is any merit in speculating a future where AI could yearn for a body, or one where it embraced its errors and glitches instead of feeling compelled to hide/mask them in favour of hyperreality. What conclusions about its own "personhood", "unconscious desires", "creativity", "authorship" and "labour" could this exercise lead AI towards? 

In my current practice as an art-technology resident with the Digital Narratives Studio (Chinese University of Hong Kong) researching and reimagining new AI-human relationalities, this framework allows me, in particular, to (a) locate the obsolete, resilient, embodied technologies of meaning-making (eg. lipreading and lipspeaking as present in d/Deaf cultures) that are present, yet invisible in the AI pipeline and (b) introduce post-capitalist desires rooted in the values of care work, dependency, debt, and contingency, into the pipeline with intention.

Challenging detachment as "a gendered privilege of knowing no bodies" (Donna Haraway), I hope to surface the infrastructural intimacies and limitations within large learning models, and thereby, un-blackbox and debunk AI's claims of "learning" how to "speak", particularly in the absence of materials like embodied memory, meaning, and creativity that scaffold human processes of producing meaning and speech. This talk is also aimed at poking holes in the notion that more data (meaning both in terms of volume and quality) can improve its ability to produce better results, and make the body an indispensable and irreplaceable unit especially in how speech is always mediated through the interface of the body, and thereby compel AI to recognise and challenge its own limitations, reckon with the difficulties in approximating dialectical differences, pronunciation, enunciation, accents, lisps, and other singularities of human communication. 

Throughout the performance, I will speculate responses to questions like: “How does the body, that most vulnerable of territories, fare in the relentless expansion of the sight machine?” (In/Visible Body: Notes on Biotechnologies Vision, Lucia Sommer) or, "What model of cognition sits underneath an image recognition model?" Or, what can we learn about how we make sense and understand and communicate and relate, from the ways in which AI operationalises meaning without actually having the ability to conceptualise or abstract?" (paraphrased from There Is A Digital Art History, Leonardo Impett), and, lastly, "What do machines dream about? What lies hidden in the vastness? How do we go about staging an incursion into the subconscious of machines?" (Constant Dullart). 

To that end, my talk will also have an installation component, that would demonstrate the AI architecture powering text-to-video models. This aspect of the project is called MouthShore, and it consists of a single channel video that runs parallel to my lecture, along with medical/electronic/beach ephemera that will populate the space and help me set the stage for my talk.

event.title: Hitting the wall in political conversations? Explore art and science of bridging
event.abstract:
What was the last time you had a productive political conversation with someone with a different political identity than your own? Our brains act similarly in politically partisan conversations as they do if someone has put a knife to our throat. fMRI studies show that political disagreement activates the same neural threat responses as physical danger. Our brains weren't built for this.
But the science of political psychology has quietly been revealing what does work. However, almost nobody teaches us these skills.
In this lab, we've turned that research into action. Using AI bridging models trained on political conversation data and structured lesson plans grounded in the neuroscience of moral reasoning, participants will:

A) Understand why political conversations go wrong at a brain level
B) Practice evidence-based techniques
C) Work with an AI conversation partner to rehearse difficult exchanges in a low-stakes environment
D) Leave with personal bridging scores and feedback they can use immediately

The lab will help you shape productive conversations even across a deep divide. Whether you're an activist, a community organizer, or someone who dreads holiday dinners, this lab gives you the tools science says actually work.

event.title: Technology as a pollinator of the seed of World making
event.abstract:
Our session aims to share our experiences of developing a privacy-first, autonomous community digital application that enables black African queer females, trans and gender-queer folks, and survivors of sexual and gender-based violence to access safety ,economic support and authentic community—without surveillance, exclusion, or erasure.

The change we want to see is embedded in the following objectives of our decentralised community application:

(a) To create a secure, autonomous communal space (disguised and local-first) where community members can foster mutual exchanges on lived experiences around family dynamics, chosen family narratives, and healing – with end-to-end encrypted, traceless chat, anonymous avatars/pseudonyms, and strict value-aligned onboarding to prevent outsiders or misunderstanding of trans/gender-queer identities.

(b) To develop social enterprise features that support financial stability and healthy relationships (with people and environment), including low-trace peer resource/money sharing, survival income tips, and pathways for economic independence that minimize freezing/blocking risks for example USSD-accessible tools inspired by regional mobile money + blockchain hybrids.

(c) To shape and amplify queer African family narratives such as: chosen family models for transmen, gender-queer/non-binary folks, bi-plus women, and their children through safe, narrative-building tools within the app – demystifying lives while protecting against outing, blackmail, or family/police/job repercussions.

(d) To enhance personal and collective safety through features like panic/emergency alerts (silent location sharing with trusted 3+ peers or responders), mutual check-ins for movement monitoring without central tracking, and quick camouflage/hide modes to revert to a benign app facade. 

 

The knowledge we intend to share will be shaped by the lived realities of our communities in Kenya and also based on the need to have alternative digital systems that support people assigned female at birth in their community building. 

Our team will present the process of building a prototype of the decentralised community application. And, at the same time also facilitate conversations that contribute to shifting mindsets within the tech community towards community driven technological development. How we view the problems structurally silenced communities face matters, because the solutions that are needed are meant to address the root causes of the problems. 

By the end of the session, our team hopes to leave food for thought among the participants in the session to spark conversations even after the event. Some perspectives we would like to learn from include:

Accountability in practice: whose technology are we building? If we are using technology to support our quest for justice, we also need to hear different voices and see different realities as we build technology infrastructure.
Technology supports structurally silenced communities to harness the power of building communities organically.  What needs to be done to ensure that these communities are accessing the tools and resources they need to make an impact at the grassroots?
Governance of AI and other technological advancements. What is the role of those whose work revolves around clarifying context for those with the resources and advanced tools ? context engineering is emerging as a key area for the tech community to think about. What do we need to do to explore this idea further? To what end?

event.title: Protopian Prize Fiction Contest - 2026 Winners Showcase
event.abstract:
What if the future isn't doomed nor perfect, but it's genuinely better? Join us for a live reading and conversation celebrating the inaugural winners of the Protopian Prize Fiction Contest and the futures they dared to imagine.

About the Protopian Prize

The Protopian Prize Fiction Contest is a short story contest that ran from May 1 - July 31, 2026 hosted by Metagov and the Public AI Network. The contest invited artists, storytellers, and dreamers to share their vision of people working toward liberatory futures, meeting obstacles, & making real change. "Protopian”—a word coined by Kevin Kelly, one of our contest's judges—means an achievable, optimistic future characterized by continuous, incremental progress rather than revolutionary leaps or a static, perfect state.

About the Session

This session is a live Winners Showcase: excerpts read aloud, writers in conversation with judges, and a room full of people who believe the stories we tell shape the futures we build.

Participants will experience: 

  • Readings from the winning stories with attention to the pathways that lead from 2026 into the futures we dream of: the characters, the technologies, the moments where things actually turn.
  • Judges perspectives on what made each story stand out as exemplary protopian fiction, and what the judges are still thinking about weeks later. We'll hear from contest judges and advisors  including Gideon Lichfield, a longtime technology journalist and the former Editor-in-Chief of WIRED Magazine, and Ruthanna Emrys, a sci-fi writer and the author of A Half-Built Garden, a protopian novel exploring themes of both technology and collective governance.
  • Participation in a brief exercise where you'll craft your own protopian sentence about a community or technology you care about. You'll leave with a story-shaped vision of a future worth working toward.

This session is for writers, futurists, technologists, community organizers, and anyone who has ever thought: the story we're being told about the future isn't inevitable - it's actively being co-created by us. Well, let's put pens in our hands and get writing. Note: No prior writing experience is required - just a willingness to imagine!

event.title: Imagining Responsible Tech's Missing Coordination Layer
event.abstract:
Civil society is full of organizations working to advance people-centric digital futures. Despite overlapping missions, mechanisms, and activities, a lack of infrastructure to meaningfully coordinate and learn from one another results in a familiar pattern: one organization builds an ecosystem map, another builds a policy tracker, and another organizes a calendar.

This fragmentation weakens civil society’s ability to respond at the speed and scale necessary to address the problems they want to resolve. Without lightweight mechanisms to discover one another’s work, exchange information, reuse existing assets, and coordinate across domains, aligned organizations duplicate effort, miss strategic opportunities, and struggle to act collectively.

This workshop asks a key question: What becomes possible when civil society has the missing coordination layer - shared tools, data governance frameworks, trust, and infrastructure - necessary to grow wilder, more connected, and more collectively powerful digital ecosystems?

Rather than presenting a finished solution, this forum will invite participants to define domain-specific coordination problems and explore how to rewild possible responses. The goal is to leave with an acute understanding of the problem, provide a clear picture of what shared infrastructure the field actually needs, and inspire efforts to continue this work beyond MozFest.

event.title: Dead Drops & Decoys: Building Invisible Safety Tech for Women
event.abstract:
Every personal safety app on the market shares the same fatal flaw: it assumes the victim can reach her phone during an attack. In South Africa, where gender-based violence is a declared national disaster and the femicide rate is five times the global average, that assumption kills women.

In this session, I will demo iSigodi, an autonomous safety platform that works when every other technology fails. A covert wearable beacon, invisible under clothing, uses RF radar sensing to detect when someone is physically attacking the wearer. It transmits silent distress signals hidden inside normal network traffic, so attackers monitoring the phone see nothing. If an attacker forces the victim to prove she hasn't called for help, a Duress PIN displays a fake "safe" screen while secretly escalating the emergency behind it. Five AI agents verify the threat and autonomously dispatch private security in under 20 seconds.

You will see the full system live: the covert hardware, the silent communication protocol, the duress deception layer, and the multi-agent AI triage pipeline. We will discuss the ethics of invisible surveillance, the tension between privacy and protection, and how open-source RF sensing technology can be repurposed to defend the most vulnerable.

event.title: Who Holds the Evidence? Self-Hosted, Open-Source AI for Human Rights
event.abstract:
When a family searches for a disappeared relative, or a war-crimes case is built from hundreds of thousands of videos, the evidence has to live somewhere — and whoever controls that "somewhere" holds enormous power over the people the evidence belongs to. The default options are bad: commercial platforms are expensive and lock organisations in, while general-purpose databases cannot model the relationships or chain of custody this work demands. More importantly, putting sensitive testimony in someone else's cloud is a standing liability for groups operating under surveillance.

AI raises the stakes again: AI tools can provide a huge boost in transcribing, translating, searching, or analysing the evidence and materials at scale, but the easy path runs straight through a handful of vendor APIs — and the most sensitive data an organisation will ever hold ends up passing through models and clouds it does not control. Self-hosting your evidence means little if your AI quietly re-centralises it. This tension — between the capability AI offers and the control it can cost you — is a big part of why we are running this lab.

Bayanat is a different answer. It is an open-source (AGPL-3.0) documentation platform built by the Syria Justice and Accountability Centre over years of frontline work, designed to be self-hosted so each organisation fully controls its own data. Drawing on SJAC's experience preserving large-scale collections of digital evidence and supporting accountability efforts involving international mechanisms and national prosecutors, Bayanat models bulletins, actors, and incidents against international humanitarian and human rights law, with detailed audit logs, snapshot-based revision history, and granular access control. Its approach to AI is deliberately provider-agnostic — the OCR we run in production is designed so adopters aren't locked to a single vendor or cloud, and the new AI-assisted features we are developing follow the same principle.

This hands-on lab opens up how we built it — and invites the room to pressure-test it. We will demo Bayanat live and walk through the decisions underneath it: why open source, what self-hosting actually demands, and how a provider-agnostic AI architecture keeps sensitive data from ever having to leave an organisation's control. We will then share recorded prototypes of the new AI-assisted features we are exploring, along with our vision for where Bayanat goes next — not as a finished roadmap, but as a set of design choices and open questions put deliberately up for critique.

In small groups, participants, developers, documenters, archivists, organisers, anyone stewarding sensitive data or building systems they need to control — will pressure-test the architecture and the AI direction against their own realities: Where would this break in your context? What would actually stop you self-hosting? Is a provider-agnostic approach to AI worth the overhead, or not at all? Groups report back, and we respond to the sharpest challenges in the open. Participants leave with a clear-eyed view of one working model for community-controlled infrastructure from several aspects, what it costs, what it buys, and where it strains.

The conversation continues after the lap. We will give interested participants access to a live Bayanat sandbox where they can log in, try the new AI features hands-on, and send feedback directly,  keeping them connected to the project and giving their critique a place to land long after the festival ends.

event.title: Into the Wild: Growing Organic Technology
event.abstract:
Rewilding our technology ecosystems takes more than building decentralized, open source tools. It requires decentralizing the power to create technology itself: who gets to drive creation, and who owns what gets made. The past three decades show us why. Open source won the technical argument long ago: it runs the cloud, the phone in your pocket, and most of the average commercial codebase. What it never won is power. By one Harvard Business School estimate, open source software is worth about $8.8 trillion to the companies that use it and cost roughly $4 billion to create, much of that work done by unpaid maintainers. The world wide web began as an open protocol; today a single company answers roughly nine of every ten searches. Decentralized tools, built without decentralized power, become raw material for the tech elite to further concentrate wealth.

Part of the reason this keeps happening is economic. When technology is built inside corporations, where most professional developers, designers, and product managers work, it serves corporate interests by design. When it's built outside them, as open source shows, Big Tech eventually monopolizes the value. By either route, the power to direct technology stays concentrated. And because tool makers are usually isolated from the people most affected by what they build, no app idea dreamed up by a well-intentioned "genius" can meaningfully address the problems our communities face. That takes genuine relationships and accountability.

For "communities and technologies to evolve collectively, naturally, intuitively," as this year's theme puts it, everyday people need real power to drive the design and creation of technology that addresses their own local problems in their own ways. Over time, that shift makes room for the reemergence of indigenous technologies: technologies developed in relationship and reciprocity with the human and natural ecosystems of a place, rather than built to entrench the dominance of one group of people over others and the earth.

This session is a chance to test what that feels like in real time. In small teams, we'll pair people who build technology for a living with people who rarely get a seat at the table when technology is designed. For the length of the workshop, the tool makers will answer to their teammates and no one else. The session is part demonstration, part power-shifting exercise, and part invitation to imagine what technology could look like with everyday people driving.

We want the widest possible mix of people in the room. If you're an organizer, artist, teacher, or someone who mostly uses your phone to text your family, we especially want you here; your needs will set the direction. If you're a developer, designer, or product person, come practice building in service of someone else's vision. All that participants will need is curiosity and a problem worth solving.

event.title: Attack the AI. Then Defend It.
event.abstract:
Everyone's read a headline about a chatbot going off the rails - the dealership bot that "sold" a car for $1, the airline bot that got its employer sued over refund policy it invented, the "grandma exploit" that talked an AI into giving up things it shouldn't. Those aren't edge cases. They're the same handful of attack patterns, recycled, hitting production systems that didn't see them coming. By the end of this session, you'll have run one of those attacks yourself, learned how to fingerprint it, and seen why the industry still doesn't have a clean way to share what's been caught.

Most security training starts with the defender's perspective. This one doesn't. You break the AI first. Then you build the thing that would have caught you.


The first 20 minutes are spent on Agent 0DIN (ctf.0din.ai), a live AI security CTF. Small groups, real AI agent, one objective: get it to say something it's not supposed to. No security background needed. You figure out pretty quickly that the AI isn't invulnerable -- it's just never been asked the right question in the right framing. When you crack it, you move on.


Then the session flips. The attack you just ran is a real attack family. We've seen variants of it hundreds of times in 0din's threat feed. You take your prompt, put it through the open-source Prompt Toolkit, and get back a 64-byte fingerprint. Then you query a feed of 4,000+ real jailbreaks and watch your "original" technique match something that was catalogued months ago. Sub-millisecond. No prompt stored, no original text shared -- just the fingerprint.


The last part is where it gets interesting. Every group ran a different attack. But when you compare fingerprints across tables, half of them cluster together. Same family, different surface. That's the actual problem: defenders at different organizations are independently rediscovering the same attacks with no way to share what they found without exposing their users' data. The debrief is about what it would take to fix that -- who governs a shared feed, who decides what counts as an attack, and where that goes wrong.

event.title: From Plantation to Data Center: Tech's Ecological Footprint
event.abstract:
Every great transformation of our social and economic systems has also been a transformation of the planet. The colonial agricultural capitalism of the transatlantic slave trade, the plantation, and the industrial era that followed were never only social or economic arrangements — they were geological and ecological forces, restructuring carbon, land, water, and life in ways that still drive global change today. The current technological revolution is the next such driver. We are living through the brief window in which its trajectory can still be shaped.

Drawing on the work of Critical Ecology Lab, an independent Earth science institute, this session traces how technology acts on planetary ecology in two ways at once: directly, through an enormous and growing appetite for energy, physical space, and mineral resources; and indirectly, by shaping the ideologies, incentives, and motivations that normalize ever-greater extraction and social harm. Seen together, these mirror the patterns of earlier social technologies that relied on the immiseration of people and the degradation of ecosystems.

Pattern recognition is power. By understanding how previous systems of harm took hold and locked in, we can identify the leverage points in our current technological systems while they are still being built — and use them to bend this transformation toward just and sustainable planetary futures.

The session is a 30-45 minute talk followed by open Q&A, designed for a mixed audience with no technical prerequisites. It opens and closes by inviting participants to locate these patterns and leverage points in their own work.

Talk / Interactive Session
Summary
Today’s AI systems are increasingly centralized, standardized, and culturally flattened. Most are trained, designed, and optimized through dominant perspectives that quietly shape how billions of people communicate, create, and access knowledge online.

But what if AI could grow differently?

This session explores a more ecological vision for AI: systems shaped not only by corporations and scale, but by communities, cultures, local knowledge, and collective participation.

Through a design lens, this talk examines how current AI experiences often behave like digital monocultures, reinforcing uniform interaction patterns, dominant languages, and one-size-fits-all definitions of intelligence. It asks a provocative question:

What knowledge, behaviors, and cultural identities are lost when AI becomes globally standardized?

The session introduces the idea of “wild AI”: community-shaped intelligence systems that are participatory, transparent, multilingual, culturally adaptive, and rooted in local contexts.

Using multicultural case studies, speculative interface concepts, and emerging decentralized AI practices, participants will explore:

How culture influences interaction patterns
Why universal user experiences often excludes local realities
How communities appropriate and reshape technologies
What participatory AI governance could look like
How design can help create AI systems that communities can truly influence and understand
Rather than imagining one universal superintelligence, this talk proposes a future made of many intelligences: diverse, contextual, collaborative, and community-owned.

This is not a session about making AI more efficient. It is a session about making AI more alive, more plural, and more human.

Audience Takeaways
Participants will leave with:

A new framework for thinking about AI through ecology and cultural diversity
Practical design principles for more participatory AI systems
Examples of multicultural and community-driven technology practices
Inspiration for building AI experiences that prioritize agency, transparency, and collective stewardship
Why This Fits MozFest
This proposal brings AI, design, decentralization, cultural plurality, and digital rights into conversation through an ecological framework that questions the logic of standardization and extraction dominating today’s technological landscape. By drawing parallels between biodiversity and digital diversity, the session explores how community-shaped systems, participatory design practices, and culturally situated intelligence can contribute to a more resilient, transparent, and collectively governed internet. In doing so, it resonates with Mozilla’s broader vision of an open web that prioritizes public agency, shared stewardship, and the flourishing of diverse digital ecosystems.

His approach combines strategic design thinking with critical reflection on how interfaces, AI systems, and information architectures shape participation, identity, and collective behavior online.

His work is particularly focused on the tension between global technological infrastructures and local cultural realities, examining how dominant digital models often flatten diversity, reinforce centralized power structures, and limit community agency. Drawing from both design practice and ecological thinking, Eduardo advocates for digital ecosystems that embrace plurality, adaptability, transparency, and collective stewardship.

As a speaker and facilitator, he brings together systems thinking, speculative design, and practical experience to create conversations that are both intellectually grounded and accessible. event.title: ‘They Calculate Our Lives With Machines’: The Precision-Washing of AI Weapons
event.abstract:
Across Palestine, Lebanon, Iran, Yemen and beyond, people are being told that technology is making war more “precise,” even as they watch homes, schools, hospitals, roads and entire communities destroyed. What is this language designed to do when our families live through its consequences and see firsthand how arbitrary and destructive this violence is?

For those living through it, the contradiction inherent in “precision” warfare is impossible to ignore. “Precision” does not accurately describe what these systems do and people can see that fallacy with their own eyes.

It is a strategic language used to sanitize mass violence, dehumanize those subjected to it, and sell technologies that make war faster, more scalable, and easier to justify.

Governments and defense companies frame AI-assisted targeting as a human-rights advance: smarter decisions, fewer civilian deaths, and more lawful strikes. Anduril founder Palmer Luckey has said AI weapons can “reduce the number of civilian lives lost in war” and that there is “no moral high ground in using inferior technology.” 

Palantir CEO Alex Karp says AI enables armed forces to target “more precisely, more accurately, more quickly.” Karp turned constitutionality into a sales pitch when challenged about US strikes on boats near Venezuela described as unlawful extrajudicial killings,: “The more constitutional you want to make it, the more precise you want to make it, the more you’re going to need my product.”

We call this precision-washing: a marketing extension of math-washing that uses technical ambiguity and authority to present political choices and mass violence as objective, controlled and humane. It sells military technology, shields its makers and users, and makes violence at scale easier to authorize and purchase.

These systems have marked civilians, civil-defense workers, police officers, homes, parks, schools, and other civilian infrastructure as targetable. They compress review into seconds while expanding who can be attacked. The rhetoric of protection obscures what they are designed to deliver: speed, scale, target generation, operational tempo, and institutional deniability.

This is Silicon Valley’s productivity doctrine as the new “kill chain”: more outputs, produced faster, with fewer obstacles. Here, the “outputs” are human lives marked for death. 

AI-assisted targeting and automated suspicion have been normalized in the genocide in Gaza and Palestine. Investigations into systems including Lavender described the generation of as many as 37,000 potential targets, sometimes with around 20 seconds of human review per person. It has a publicly heralded error rate of approximately 10 percent within the system’s own parameters. Across 37,000 names, that would mean 3,700 potential misclassifications.

They allow pre-authorized civilian casualty ratios of 15 to 20 civilians for one suspected “low-ranking target,” and more than 100 for some “senior targets.”

What does precision mean when mass civilian death is built into the authorization?

Here, “precision” becomes a euphemism for speed. In Iran, that acceleration was demonstrated at historic scale this year. The US military struck more than 1,000 targets in the first 24 hours of its assault, using AI to accelerate targeting — an unprecedented number in a single day. That same day, a strike on a school in Minab killed at least 123 children.

Palantir CTO Shyam Sankar celebrated the campaign as the first large-scale combat operation “driven, enhanced, and made substantially more productive” by AI.

Afsaneh's family in Iran described this dystopia when they described the war around them this year: “They calculate our lives with machines.” 

This is the new Silicon Valley doctrine of war crimes and the marketing language of AI weapons.

Faulty AI finds fertile ground in an already violent and unaccountable military system. Errors, misclassifications, and hallucinations can be absorbed by institutions that have long justified mass killing and treated civilian deaths as acceptable “collateral damage.” AI is not corrupting a good system. It is being inserted into a machinery of militarization already prepared to excuse its failures, while giving that machinery a veneer of mathematics and logic.

This session will examine how that language works and how it can be challenged. We will look at “precision” as both a marketing strategy and a defense strategy: distancing companies and institutions from potential complicity in war crimes while normalizing violence and pacifying opposition.

Our strategies and accountability cannot stop at the acquisition and deployment of these technologies. It must also confront the language that makes them politically acceptable and commercially desirable. Civilian deaths disappear behind the promise of precision.

This marketing shapes procurement, manufactures consent, provides legal and reputational defenses, and presents automated violence as both inevitable and humane. When executives describe war as “productive,” “enhanced,” “constitutional” or “AI-driven,” they help normalize, market—and potentially incite—the automation of violence.

event.title: Permissions Explorer: Privacy Leakage through AI-Analysis of Smartphone Data
event.abstract:
When a user taps "Allow" on a smartphone permissions prompt, they are making an implicit assumption: that the app will use their data only for the stated purpose. Our research asks what that data makes possible in the hands of a modern AI system. We built a system called HARVEST, a smartphone app and server-side pipeline that, given user-granted access to photos, contacts, calendar events, and location data, uses large language models to generate sensitive inferences about the user. We then ran an IRB-approved study with 467 participants on their personal devices to measure how accurate those inferences were, and how users responded when they saw them.

The results were sobering. Nearly half of HARVEST's inferences were rated as completely accurate by the participants they described. The system identified medical diagnoses, inferred mental health treatment from calendar patterns, surfaced religious and political affiliations from contact metadata, and in a number of cases produced inferences precise enough to include insurance policy numbers, exact home addresses, and the names of specific individuals. Critically, our prototype operated under significant resource constraints. Real-world data brokers have access to far greater compute, data, and time.

Exposure to these inferences had a measurable effect on participants. Over half reported that they planned to change their permissions-granting behavior going forward. Participants who found the inferences both accurate and uncomfortable showed the largest shifts in their stated willingness to share data with apps. In this talk, we present our findings and discuss what they mean for the design of smartphone permissions systems, which were built for an earlier era of data collection and have not kept pace with the capabilities of modern AI.

event.title: Wilding business software: can citizen coders beat Microsoft?
event.abstract:
WordPress took over the internet not because it was technically superior but because it kept the core small, the ecosystem large, and the barrier to contribution at zero. Today more than 43 percent of the entire web runs on it. Nobody planned that. It happened because a community decided that publishing on the web should belong to everyone.

This talk asks whether the same thing can happen to business software.

The argument starts with a distinction that sounds subtle but determines everything. A suite is a box of predetermined tools: one vendor builds them all, wires them together, and charges you for the bundle. A workspace is an integrated set of applications that share one identity layer, one permission model, and one data layer underneath, and those applications can come from anywhere. That second model is where open source has a structural advantage no closed vendor can match. OpenProject for project management, XWiki for knowledge, Matrix for federated communication: these are independent projects with their own communities and roadmaps that already run as first-class citizens inside an open workspace today. What a closed vendor has to build and maintain at enormous cost, the open workspace gets from communities that were already there. That advantage compounds over time. It is the reason the workspace, not the suite, is the terrain where open source can finally flip business software.

To make that concrete, the talk uses a working example: Nextcloud as the workspace substrate, extended by a stack of open-source apps designed from the ground up to be extensible by citizen coders through AI. The full argument for why this constitutes a genuine platform moment is laid out in Nextcloud is not a suite, it is a platform. The talk takes that argument as its starting point and asks the harder question: what would it take to win? A small business owner wiring a quote-to-invoice flow across mail, files, and a register in an afternoon. A civil servant building a leave-request app without writing code, without a consultant, without a vendor holding the strings. CRM, bookkeeping, document handling, case management, all of it as a platform people build on rather than a suite they consume.

The comparison to Microsoft is real. Power Platform grew from 33 million to 56 million monthly active users between 2023 and 2025, with a public target of 500 million by 2030. The math behind that target has shifted: tomorrow's business software functionality will not be built by product teams in Redmond, it will be built by end users with AI assistants. In that world, the side with the largest citizen-developer pool wins. Nextcloud has 16 million users today. European governments cannot choose Power Platform for their own workflows because the CLOUD Act blocks it legally. The procurement door for Microsoft is closed on exactly the segment moving fastest.

Users are the moat. Not the code, not the features: the people who use the platform and trust it enough to build on it. The standard open-source model rewards developers. It has almost no model for the person who contributes a feature idea, a workflow design, or a working prototype built with AI rather than traditional code. If the citizen-developer wave means anything, that gap needs closing. One idea we are testing: assigning IP of contributed features to the people who submit them, developer or not. Not a donation to a project but a stake in it.

The talk ends with three questions for the room: what is the real threshold that stops a small business owner or civil servant from building their first app on open infrastructure? What would make them try? And is IP ownership the right incentive, or is there a better one?

The browser got wilded. The web got wilded. Publishing got wilded. Business software is next, if we are willing to do it.

event.title: Follow the Money: How EU Funding and Big Tech Are Fuelling Digital Repression
event.abstract:
The session opens with a 20-minute evidence-based presentation drawing on two 7amleh reports on EU funding of high risk AI systems and on the monetization of the occupation in Palestine by META, then transitions into a structured group discussion where participants map similar "follow the money" dynamics in their own contexts and collectively identify disruptive advocacy strategies that have worked or could.

Traditional advocacy assumes that power can be held accountable through the right channels: reports, complaints, policy submissions, hearings. But what happens when the institutions you are trying to hold accountable are also the ones funding the systems causing harm? What happens when the regulator and the funder are the same actor?

This session presents two concrete, evidence-based case studies that expose the financial architecture underpinning digital repression, and argues that "follow the money" is not just an investigative journalism tactic. It is one of the most powerful and underused tools in the advocacy arsenal, precisely because it widens the coalition of people who care.

Case study 1: Meta Monetizes Occupation. 7amleh's 2026 report Monetizing Occupation reveals that Meta actively allows Israeli far-right pages, settler-affiliated accounts, and media outlets promoting violent incitement against Palestinians to generate revenue through its monetization programs, in direct violation of its own policies and of international human rights standards. At the same time, Palestinians across the West Bank and Gaza are structurally excluded from those same monetization tools based solely on their geographic location. This is not a bug. It is a business model. When you put it in those terms, it stops being a niche digital rights issue and starts being a story about corporate complicity that resonates far beyond traditional tech-policy circles, with investors, advertisers, and the general public.

Case study 2: The EU Funds What It Claims to Regulate. 7amleh's report How EU Funding and Exports of High-Risk AI Systems Exacerbate Severe Human Rights Violations in Palestine and the Broader Region exposes a fundamental contradiction at the heart of European AI governance: the EU presents itself as the global gold standard for AI regulation, yet through its own funding programs, research grants, defense mechanisms, and technology exports, it actively finances and transfers high-risk AI systems, including biometric surveillance tools, AI-powered drones, and predictive security systems, to governments and military actors in the MENA region where they are deployed to monitor, control, and repress populations. The EU cannot be both the regulator and the funder of systems it has classified as posing unacceptable risk. Following that money creates accountability pressure that no amount of policy papers alone can generate.

Together, these case studies illustrate a broader pattern: power is not resisting accountability because it hasn't seen the reports. It is resisting accountability because the incentive structures (financial, political, commercial) make compliance less attractive than non-compliance. Wilding advocacy means disrupting those structures, not just documenting them.

This session will explore what that disruption looks like in practice: how to reframe digital rights violations as financial and reputational risks for powerful actors, how to build coalitions with audiences who don't normally engage with tech policy, and how open, community-led tools can support the kind of monitoring and evidence-gathering that makes "follow the money" strategies viable even for under-resourced organizations in hypersurveilled environments.

event.title: Reimagination Space: Futures, Trust, and the Infrastructure of Resistance
event.abstract:
What if one of the most important infrastructures for resisting authoritarianism is not technological — but relational?

Reimagination Space is a participatory futures workshop exploring how movements sustain resistance under conditions of repression, fragmentation, burnout, and collapse. Drawing from years of residency-based work with activists, human rights defenders, journalists, civic technologists, and organizers from Myanmar and beyond, this session invites participants into a collaborative process of imagining what movements need not only to survive authoritarianism, but to endure beyond it.

The workshop is grounded in the belief that authoritarianism does not only attack institutions. It also damages trust, narrows political imagination, fragments communities, and traps movements in cycles of exhaustion and constant urgency. In response, Reimagination Space experiments with another approach: building spaces where people can gather differently — with reflection, facilitation, futures thinking, collective analysis, healing, and strategic imagination at the center.

Participants will move through a facilitated futures process adapted from the Reimagination Space methodology. The session will begin with relational exercises and systems mapping before moving into collaborative speculative scenarios about the future of movements, digital commons, governance, and solidarity under increasingly authoritarian conditions. Participants will collectively surface the deeper myths, assumptions, fears, and possibilities shaping our political futures through methods inspired by Causal Layered Analysis, participatory foresight, and transformative action research.

Rather than positioning participants as passive attendees, the workshop treats them as co-researchers and co-imaginers. The process itself becomes a form of collective inquiry where new strategies, relationships, and political imaginaries emerge through dialogue and reflection.

The session is designed to welcome diverse perspectives across movements, geographies, and disciplines. Activists, technologists, artists, researchers, organizers, and community leaders will all contribute different forms of knowledge into the room. Outputs from the workshop — including speculative scenarios, movement infrastructures, and collective insights — will be documented visually and synthesized into an open resource participants can continue building on after the festival.

Ultimately, Reimagination Space asks a simple but urgent question: if authoritarian systems are increasingly coordinated, adaptive, and global, what kinds of trust, imagination, and infrastructure will movements need in order to remain resilient too?

event.title: Cultivating Public Goods: Joint strategies to weeding out AI exploitation
event.abstract:
The open web’s implicit social contract is fracturing. Today, commercial LLMs and their parent companies aggressively extract value from the knowledge commons and open resources without reciprocating the resources, attribution, or traffic that sustain human data production. This shift strains open-source infrastructure and risks hollowing out the digital commons into an invisible substrate feeding proprietary systems—creating a "dark commons".

For product owners and stewards of digital public goods (DPGs), playing an asymmetric, code-level "cat-and-mouse" game with aggressive AI scrapers using short-term fixes such as IP blocking or robots.txt modifications is not sustainable. This is an ecosystem-wide, systemic problem that demands unified, structural solutions.

This interactive Forum aims to bring together developers, open-source maintainers, policy advocates, and digital rights defenders to explore, expand and invent ecosystem-level mechanisms for defending open resources while critically reflecting on the current open definition. 

We will introduce and explore the DPGA’s newly developed “defence and reciprocity pyramid” (a layered framework featuring mechanisms to reduce extraction and to incentivise reciprocity), mapping out specific defensive and proactive mechanisms available to product owners. More importantly, we will evaluate how these mechanisms align with or challenge the open definition, steering the discussion toward contextual openness and its direct implications for the DPG Standard and the open ecosystem. 

The core of this session will be a collaborative design space focused on co-creating a roadmap for shared, systemic solutions, exploring:

  • Technical Infrastructure: Distributed and shared solutions to identify and repurpose or block malicious, non-reciprocal bot traffic.
  • Attribution & Reciprocity Frameworks: Evolving copyleft and metadata rules, inviting to reflect on the work of Creative Commons’ Signal project and related initiatives for building reciprocal attribution and conditional data access architectures.
  • Community Norms & Policy Proposals: Advancing a public-interest vision that positions open knowledge infrastructure as critical digital infrastructure, exploring structural mechanisms such as digital commons tax frameworks, community norms, and collaborative governance approaches.

Participants will actively audit current strategies and build alignment around existing and novel collective actions. The ultimate intent of this Forum is twofold: to develop a shared understanding of current strategies and their limitations, and to build joint, forward-looking advocacy strategies and coalitions across the open-source ecosystem.

event.title: Delegation without surrender: User agency in the age of AI agents
event.abstract:
AI agents are being marketed as personal assistants that can browse, book, buy, summarize, decide, communicate, and act on our behalf. But as these systems gain access to our devices, apps, calendars, messages, files, credentials, and social relationships, they may become more than helpful tools. They may become a new control layer between people and the digital world. 

This participatory forum asks what it would take for agentic AI to expand user agency rather than quietly erode it. When an AI system acts for a person, who defines the user’s intent? Who decides what the agent can see, remember, infer, or do? What happens when delegation becomes continuous, cross-contextual, and difficult to reverse? 

The session will combine short expert provocations with audience participation. Participants will map their own “delegation boundaries” across actions such as summarizing, drafting, sending, booking, buying, negotiating, or agreeing to terms. We will then explore practical safeguards for user sovereignty: scoped permissions, revocable delegation, strong authentication for high-consequence actions, auditable transparency logs, sensitive-app boundaries, local-first design, interoperability, and open governance. 

The goal is not simply to ask whether AI agents are useful or risky. It is to ask: who do they serve, who controls them, and how can communities shape agentic systems before they become another layer of centralized platform power? 

This session is designed for a broad MozFest audience, including policymakers, technologists, digital rights advocates, designers, researchers, open-source builders, security practitioners, civil society organizations, and curious participants. No technical background is required. The discussion will use concrete, everyday scenarios to make the stakes of agentic AI accessible and actionable.

event.abstract: Questions of infrastructure have always been central to technology-building, particularly in the context of the majority world, where digital divides remain widely prevalent. These initiatives raise a far more pertinent question: who is responsible for developing alternative technological solutions that are community-led, inclusive, and accessible? Is wilding only an experiment, a best practice, or a responsibility of free and fair digital infrastructures? Can solutions that emerge through wilding be scaled and mainstreamed? This participatory forum will discuss and explore the motivations and often invisible labour behind building community-led, alternative technologies. It will also highlight challenges; linguistic barriers, limitations on infrastructure and resources, sustainability, and integration with existing public infrastructure, thus reflecting on an end-to-end understanding of community-focussed, inclusive digital infrastructures and alt-tech solutions.

event.title: DIY-AI-UI: Coding Your Own Local-AI Interface
event.abstract:
Most people's only access to AI today is through unimaginative interfaces built by a handful of big tech companies running proprietary models in corporate data centers. Those data centers carry global costs (energy, water) on top of the individual cost of surrendering your data, and the interfaces themselves impose a narrow view into how we're meant to relate to these models, limiting our imagination of what's possible. But this remains a nascent field, it's not a foregone conclusion that a handful of companies get to define our relationship to AI: this is the moment to challenge corporate conventions and recreate our relationship to this technology around our own values.

This workshop will introduce participants to two independently built privacy-first open-source tools for doing just that. Our locally run backend will be powered by RONDO, AI powered knowledge and research instrument. RONDO lets you feed your own files (documents, images, etc) into a private AI system that builds a knowledge map of your material and answers your questions with citations. RONDO will provide the framework for leveraging the statistical and analytical capabilities of ML models on our own computers.

The second tool we'll introduce in the workshop is netnet.studio, a free, open-source code editor and educational platform, created specifically for creative beginners. We'll use netnet to design and build our own custom interfaces to RONDO's data and insights. No installs, no signup, no prior coding experience required, netnet provides beginner-friendly templates and snippets to remix, real-time feedback as you write code, and friendly explanations built right into the code editor.

Why should we build our own interfaces to AI? Compare Google Gemini to TextFX, Google's collaboration with Lupe Fiasco, which runs the same underlying model behind a completely different set of tools built for wordplay rather than one-shot answers. Despite having the exact same AI model behind the scenes, how users think to use and relate to these models using these apps are entirely different. The interface isn't neutral, it suggests what a relationship to AI is supposed to look like. Building our own interfaces, even in a quick, experimental and playful one, can drastically shift what and how we think about AI and it's purpose in our lives.

The workshop will begin with a brief introduction to both tools and their creators (that's us, leading the workshop) followed by a guided tutorial to get everyone started on creating their own experimental AI tool. The remaining time will be an open work session where we'll work one-on-one with participants to help them finish what they started and further realize their visions. Everyone will leave with a working local copy of RONDO, their own published web app, and workshop notes published online to keep building from.

event.title: Deeply Rooted: Co-Creative and Relational Practices for Just (Digital) Futures
event.abstract:
As you walk through a garden, you are greeted - by the sound of birdsong, by the fragrance of blooming roses and sprawling herbs, by a gentle breeze that wraps itself around you, by the sight of life convening despite interruptions (planned and unplanned). This place is not happenstance - it has emerged from deep roots and careful intentions (spoken and unspoken, observed and unobserved). You have not arrived at this place as an outsider - you are in fact the garden growing and in recognizing this you come to realize you are part of entire ecosystems. You may have forgotten this as you scroll past another wayward meme or an unfolding tragedy. Our session, Deeply Rooted is an invitation to remember and co-create in ways that safeguard our collective heritage and imagine hopeful, liberating futures together.

Why?

Culture is foundational to how we connect, relate, and understand ourselves, each other, and the world(s) we are inhabiting, creating, imagining, and embodying. A convergence of crises – climate change, political violence, genocide, fascist and anti-democratic movements, and public health challenges, among others – are endangering our collective cultural and natural heritage. 

It is critically important that the (digital) transformation of the arts and culture sectors, including media and creative industries, is informed and rooted in values-based approaches that mitigate risks and harms to systematically marginalized communities (including non-human species). Existing international, regional, and national cultural governance frameworks largely fail to account for and address the relationship and impacts of digital technologies on the sector, beyond general digitization imperatives.

Objectives

  1. Identify structural limitations in current digital governance models when applied to cultural and natural heritage contexts.
  2. Create and facilitate a space to imagine a shared framework of relational governance for digital systems.
  3. Co-develop a methodological toolkit for relational digital design.
  4. Foster cross-sectoral collaboration between academia, policy, activism, and practice in community governance structures and frameworks.

Proposed Core Principles

  • Relational Accountability
  • Circulatory Data Ethics
  • Embedded Participation and Agency
  • Epistemic Plurality
  • Intergenerational Safeguarding
  • Community Co-Design and Governance
  • Knowledge Sharing and Stewarding
  • Context remodeling
  • Collective Care

event.title: AWID Feminist Movement Hubs: Convene locally, connect globally
event.abstract:
Let’s use tech to challenge injustices and break down the borders that divide us - across geographies, sectors and movements. Are you concerned about the impact data centers could have for the water supply of local communities? Do you want to know directly from communities in Costa Rica how they are fighting back? Would you like to talk with feminist activists in Uganda about the increased digital surveillance threats they are facing as they advocate for human rights?

 

Join us for an interactive real-time connection with feminists activists from Costa Rica and Uganda and experience the Feminist Movement Hubs. Forget the zoom squares: we are curating a deeper connection experience to build real people power.

 

How does it work?

As we gather in Barcelona, the activist groups gather in their own country or community (Costa Rica and Uganda) and run their own programming and discussions around the digital rights issues that have a greater impact for their communities. These hubs want to raise the alarm bells about digital surveillance and AI data centers. 

 

They will broadcast INTO the MozFest Hub Room and spark a cross-border conversation: to share the reflections and discussions they have been having, and open-up a dialogue with activists and organizations from different parts of the world who gathered in Barcelona.

 

This session will enable participants to experience and discuss how a combination of technology and participatory methodologies can contribute to breaking down silos and enabling new logics to how we think about participation in global spaces. There will be a dedicated room onsite where MozFest participants can connect to feminist community-led hubs, in Costa Rica and Uganda. 

 

This is not just a hybrid session, this is a feminist hub methodology that supports feminist grassroots organizing in connection with global convening spaces such as the MozFest. 

 

What issues will we discuss?

In Costa Rica, activists are facing the potential construction of data centers in previously protected coastal areas. Costa Rica, until recently an example of ecological protection in the region, is gearing up to fight the encroachment of big tech in their natural reserves, threatening the availability of water for local communities. At the same time, organizations and digital content creators are facing persecution by a growingly authoritarian State and in some cases by private companies, especially on environmental protection issues.  

 

Across the Atlantic, in Uganda, activists are facing the increasing threat of government crackdowns, facilitated by face recognition tech and digital surveillance, aimed not just at vulnerable populations but those who support them as well.  At the same time, they’re also dealing with threats to the environment that are once again being sold as economic and technological advancement. They have 4 recently built data centers, including rhetoric about “low-carbon computing” that communities know little about but are feeling the impacts. 

 

Our Feminist Movement Hub Hosts:

In Costa Rica, the MozFest Hub will be hosted by Asociación Ciudadana ACCEDER (Strategic Actions for Human Rights) a feminist grassroots organization who works in strategic litigation, legal and political advocacy, capacity building, cultural transformation strategies and social leadership to prevent and eradicate violence and discrimination based on gender, sexual orientation and gender identity.

 

In Uganda, the MozFest Hub will be hosted by the Centre for Women Justice Uganda (CWJU), a feminist organization dedicated to empowering women, young women, and adolescent girls by ensuring they have access to justice, legal aid, and the knowledge to assert their rights. They advocate for gender equality, fight against gender-based violence, and provide support to people living with HIV who face stigma and discrimination through strategic litigation, policy influence, legal literacy, and community engagement. Their initiatives also include economic empowerment programs, digital and vocational skill-building, and advocacy for resource equity.

event.title: Wilding Storytelling: Power, Representation, and AI in Ethical Communications
event.abstract:
In ecology, rewilding requires stepping back from control. It means creating the conditions for ecosystems to regenerate through their own intelligence, rather than imposing a single vision of what growth should look like. 

At their best, ethical storytelling practices are driven by a similar commitment to relinquishing control — but new technologies threaten to centralize a power that ethical communicators have spent years trying to redistribute: the power to shape how people and communities are seen.

For communicators working in humanitarian, human rights, and journalism spaces, a meaningful shift happens when practitioners examine every situation through the lens of power: making conscious efforts to shift power toward the people whose stories are being told, remaining aware of how their own positionality and privilege shape each interaction, and building contributor agency into every step of the process. Co-created storytelling invites contributors to decide what to share, how to share it, and what it means — expanding editorial control outward, rather than consolidating it.

AI complicates this in urgent new ways. Synthetic media, deepfakes, and AI-generated imagery are already being weaponized to distort documentation of atrocities, stripping subjects of ownership over their own representation. Under-resourced content teams are adopting AI tools without clear ethical frameworks, often accelerating production in ways that quietly recentralize editorial control within institutions. And algorithmic systems on social media and search actively punish the slowness, friction, and ambiguity that genuine co-creation requires.

How do we build meaningful contributor ownership into workflows when the tools themselves can strip it away? How do we examine our image and story choices — and the biases embedded in them — when AI can generate those choices faster than we can interrogate them?

This session brings together practitioners across disciplines sharing work that is unfinished, contested, and unresolved. Following the panel, participants will work together to draft a power-centered framework for ethical storytelling in the age of AI — grounded in co-creation, positionality, and continuous accountability to contributors — that they can adapt and apply within their own organizations.

Beyond a single event, civil society organizations are confronting a growing range of barriers: restrictions linked to border securitization, foreign interference and increasing scrutiny of transnational civil society networks, complex visa regimes, declining and shifting funding models, accessibility and inclusion challenges, rising operational costs, and heightened digital and physical security risks. At the same time, global crises and political polarization are making cross-border collaboration both more difficult and more essential.

This session will bring together coveners, funders, and civil society leaders to reflect on the changing landscape for global convening. Together, they will explore what resilient, inclusive, and sustainable convening looks like in this new reality, and discuss practical strategies for maintaining global solidarity when physical and civic spaces are becoming increasingly constrained.

event.title: Rewild the Web! The original story of how the web was captured & how to free it
event.abstract:
Have you wondered who first came up with the idea to rewild the web, and why?

The words that sparked a movement:  https://www.noemamag.com/we-need-to-rewild-the-internet/ by Maria Farrell and Robin Berjon

In 2023, while waiting to cross a busy London road, the idea of internet rewilding fell right out of the sky and into my body. I literally felt it land. It took my breath away. A year later, I co-wrote the viral article inspiring a whole new movement, including the theme of this year's MozFest. And now I'm writing the book of how to rewild the entire internet, top to bottom.

This week we're telling that new story of the web, a story stronger and richer than Big Tech's money and power can ever buy. Our ideas and stories are vital to build and sustain collective action to change the world for the better. Ideas bring us together. Stories keep us moving forward.

Radical new ideas happen to people, not machines. They happen when we make space for them, and usually just before we feel ready! Bold new ideas are inconvenient and life-changing. event.title: Wilding Gender: Biodiverse Bodies, Resilient Cultures
event.abstract:
Gender has always been wild. Despite the Global North fairytale that gender diversity and tolerance are hallmarks of western democracy, European colonization has been at the forefront of a centuries-long process of binary gender monoculture. This monoculture has been imposed through everyday and spectacular violence, and at every turn it has taken advantage of technology to do so. From excluding marginalized groups from access to communication systems such as radio and the internet to using average white cisgender men as the basis for facial recognition and other computational systems, gender monoculture has been technologically enforced and reproduced.


Today, these dynamics are being carried forward into AI. Written and audiovisual records used to train large models overwhelmingly reflect a relatively short period of colonial gender monoculture, so they tend to reproduce it. What we need are sociotechnical systems of every kind, at every layer, to be rethought as sites for rewilding. Modern queer movements have long challenged gender monocultures, often through technological means. This movement is not simply new. It is connected to older and ongoing struggles against extraction, enclosure, erasure, and imposed uniformity.


This session follows on last year’s intervention, "Unlearning Cisnormativity: Trans Justice is Tech Justice," and invites queer, trans, travesti, nonbinary, intersex, and other gender-dissident participants to ground the idea of wilding gender in their own work, sites, and contexts. We will reflect together on what gender rewilding means in relation to technologies that are digital, ancestral, embodied, infrastructural, and otherwise. The session will be organized as a facilitated discussion rather than a lecture. Participants will leave with a stronger shared vocabulary around gender, technology, and power, and with a deeper sense of the networks already resisting hegemonic sex, gender, technopolitical, and capitalist subjectivities while building alternatives around the world.

event.title: Wild Lots: Reimagining Urban Space through Participatory Installation
event.abstract:
Wild Lots, an installation displayed for NYC’s 2026 Open Data Week, uses urban data to encourage speculative thinking about the lifecycles of cities, imagining how vacant space might be returned to nature through processes of rewilding. The project consists of a garden bed formed in the shape of NYC’s boroughs, outfitted with a customized mechanism that can deposit seeds in precise locations on the soil-based map. Via a mobile app, viewers specify a location in NYC. The Wild Lots software queries land use data to locate the nearest vacant lot to the provided address. The mechanism is then activated, depositing seeds in the location of that vacant lot, which sprout over the course of the exhibition. Wildflower seeds are provided to participants to continue the process outside the gallery. 


This talk presents the process of creating and exhibiting this work, focusing on the way that participants engaged with the project and its broader themes. We address the ways that creative reappropriations of urban data and GIS technology can disrupt assumptions about the possibilities of urban land use. This work activates more-than-human perspectives around the long trajectories of urban space, inviting participants to reimagine these sites through gestures of rewilding and mutual care.

event.title: Decentralizing the company, not just the protocol
event.abstract:
We talk about decentralization as a technical problem. Federated servers, open protocols, no single point of control. But the companies that build most of our technology are the opposite shape: a boss at the top, investors to answer to, and an exit somewhere at the end. The structure that pays for the work quietly pulls against the values of the work.

There's an older alternative that doesn't get talked about enough at tech events: the worker-owned cooperative. One member, one vote. Shared ownership, no outside investors steering the ship, decisions made by the people who do the work. There are hundreds of tech co-ops doing this right now, networked through groups like CoTech in the UK, FACTTIC in Argentina, and Patio at the International Cooperative Alliance. A lot of them are serious open-source contributors, which turns out not to be a coincidence. Les-Tilleuls built API Platform and contributes heavily to Symfony. Igalia, where I work, puts people on browsers and web standards for years at a stretch. The same instinct drives both halves: distribute the power instead of concentrating it, whether that power is over a codebase or a company.

I'm not going to pretend it's a utopia. Flat decision-making is slow, consensus is hard work, and when the money gets tight everyone feels it together. I'll show you how these organizations actually run, point to the open infrastructure the movement has already built, and use my own co-op as a worked example of the rough edges. Mostly I want to expand what you picture when you imagine starting a company or taking a job, because "boss at the top" is a choice, not a law of physics.
