event.title: Wild Roots: Climate Yoga as Embodied Environmental Education
event.abstract:
What if learning about climate change required no screens, no slides, and no prior knowledge: only a body and a patch of ground?

Wild Roots is a climate education experience rooted in yoga's oldest instructions. Ahimsa, non-harming, starts inward, no forcing, no judging what the body can't yet do, before it extends outward to the ecosystems we're trying to protect. Aparigraha, non-possessiveness, is why this practice needs nothing bought: no mat, no studio, no membership, just breath and ground.

Grounding, here, means two things at once: reconnecting to your own physical body, and stepping back from the technology that usually mediates your relationship to everything else. Before we take on the big problems, the climate, the systems, the screens, we have to relearn the more basic thing underneath them: what it feels like to simply be in a body, on the ground, breathing. From there, we work step by step, breath by breath, toward understanding what's actually sustainable, what has longevity, what will hold up for our minds, our bodies, and the ecosystems we live inside of, not as a one-time insight, but as a practice you can return to daily, the same way you return to your breath. Over time, it gets easier, more natural, and the benefits compound.

Throughout the practice, we play sounds from around the world, wind, water, birdsong, the actual voices of the ecosystems we're learning about, so participants aren't just hearing facts, they're hearing what's at stake.

Following the session, a share-out time with guided questions, resources, and thoughts on each topic is offered. When participants return to the policy table or their computers, they carry that relationship in their bodies. This is climate education for the rest of the brain, the part that moves.

Leveraging our own experiences building knowledge platforms that range from movement-informed critical analysis to artistic and creative interventions, we invite participants to work with us through a set of practical and conceptual questions: How do we navigate the tradeoffs between rigor and accessibility, advancing critical analysis that is legible to broad audiences? What does it take to sustain knowledge projects outside institutional funding and control? How do we build across languages, geographies, and different relationships to technology?

Most people encounter technology through the terms set by the institutions that build and profit from it. The frameworks for understanding digital systems — who they serve, what they obscure, what alternatives might look like — are rarely developed by or with the communities most affected by them. What would it mean to build that capacity ourselves, rooted in our own contexts and needs?

The session will be structured around a dialogue between Disjunctions and Decifer founders on lessons learned and the questions they raise, followed by group discussion and collective mapping, providing space for participants to bring their own experiences of building community knowledge interventions. The goal is to leave with something actionable: a clearer sense of what this kind of infrastructure requires, a set of connections with others working on similar questions, and concrete opportunities to plug into Disjunctions and Decifer’s critical tech literacy work.

event.title: The Witch and the Engineer: Hybrid Divination for the AI Age
event.abstract:
Divination and computation share an origin problem. Both claim to extract meaningful signal from a world that resists legibility. The tarot reader and the machine learning engineer are both in the business of pattern recognition, probability, and interpretation, yet only one of them gets to call their black box a science. This lab takes that asymmetry seriously, as both a critique and an artistic method.


The session is built around a hybrid technique I have developed over six years of artistic research at the Digital Witchcraft Institute: pairing the Marseille tarot, one of the oldest continuous cartomantic traditions in the West, with a custom JavaScript oracle I built from a corpus of oneiric testimonials and geomancy coordinates. Together, they form what I call digital artisanship: small, surreal, embodied, non-extractive software made against the industry's demand for scalability and efficiency.


The lab opens with a short framing on the shared lineage of divination and computation, and on why artisanal software is a political act in the current moment. I then perform a live hybrid reading on a figure from the AI industry, with the room helping choose the subject on the day. Cards are drawn in front of the audience, the oracle runs in parallel, and interpretation happens out loud.


Participants then take the tools into their own hands. Working in small groups, each cluster selects an industry figure of their own choice, whether a CEO, a regulator, a founder they admire or distrust, or themselves as technologists, and performs a reading using both the cards and the oracle. I move between groups offering interpretive guidance. We close by surfacing what the room produced: not predictions, but a shared exercise in unmaking the false neutrality of computation by sitting it next to its older sibling.


The lab is rooted in my decade of work in public interest technology, at Riseup Networks, Derechos Digitales, Article 19, and currently coordinating commons care for free and open source software projects at NLnet within the EU's Next Generation Internet initiative. The Witch and the Engineer is the artistic counterpart to that infrastructural work: a reminder that the people building the alternatives also need ritual, play, and weird methods of seeing.

event.title: I Was 15. Now I Run the Camp: Youth Security and Privacy Education That is Fun
event.abstract:
What does it take to run a security and privacy camp that teenagers actually want to come back to? If you've been wanting to build something similar in your own community, this session shows you how.

Two years ago, we experimented with bringing teens together over Raspberry Pis, Linux terminals, and way too much pizza and shawarma. That became JOSA CyberCamp. Across two editions, participants built a Wi-Fi handshake sniffer, a pocket-sized ad blocker, and a USB malware sanitizer. The community mattered as much as the tech: alumni still meet, collaborate on open source projects, and keep showing up long after camp ends.

This session pulls back the curtain on how it came together. Makram, who joined at 15 and became a co-organizer at 16, shares an honest account of what worked, what didn't, and what he wished existed before he started. You'll see working hardware from camp projects, then walk through curriculum and how to build a lasting community.

What started as a co-designed experiment can become a shared blueprint. Join us in shaping what comes next, so other communities can build their own CyberCamp. We will publish an open source, reusable/adaptable framework after MozFest for anyone interested.

event.title: Fables and Futures: Stories, Technology and Society
event.abstract:
In this MozFest session, participants will engage with Fables and Futures, a creative learning kit that uses a set of graphic fables, project-based activities, and a beginner-friendly game-building environment (similar to Scratch) to help young people develop a real point of view about the emerging technologies shaping their lives.

The session moves through three phases. First, participants will read one of two graphic fables set in the world of Massa Mist, a lush valley with technologies embedded in the natural landscape. Both stories are fables about surveillance, data ownership, privacy, algorithmic consent, and who gets to make decisions that affect a whole community. Following the reading, participants will reflect and debrief: who benefited, who was harmed, and what agreements should the community have in place. Participants will then encounter the real-world and historical parallels: social media recommendation algorithms, the 23andMe biometric data breach, the NSA's PRISM program, etc.

Lastly, participants will be provided with a set of diverse activities that support them to explore the themes and implications they experienced, and create their own unique artifacts. Activities include future forecasting, comic strip creation, character design and creative computation in GameBender, a play-based creative coding environment where they can build their own Massa Mist inspired games using visual "code stickers," without needing prior coding experience.

The session will culminate in a quick moment of collective production: in about 20 minutes, participants will transform the learnings, proposals, and tensions that emerged during the theatrical process into a brief policy brief in fanzine format. event.title: Rewilding Our Gardens: Communal Governance in Tech Accountability Projects
event.abstract:
Overview
The funding crisis of 2025 did not emerge from thin air. Over years of scarcity and uneven battles, small civil society groups have gone to extraordinary lengths to ensure their work endures. But our stories of survival and strategies of resilience are often left unshared.

Many grassroots initiatives still feel they are struggling alone in the face of crushing pressures. Tech accountability efforts in particular face pressure to lower their standards, to accept more corporate funding, to automate cognitive and creative labor, to put survival before community, or to surrender entirely. Too often, these dynamics remain invisible until it’s too late.

This session aims to overcome those inhibitions within a community of trust. The main question we will tackle is: How can small civil society initiatives grow and thrive in a landscape of adversity?

We will dissect moments of existential uncertainty participants have faced over the past two years and break down how they emerged from them intact. Our exploration will take us through concrete strategies and structures of renewal that are taking root in our community: co-leadership, pooled resources, mutual aid partnerships, collective project governance, “degrowth,” and internal policies that reinforce equity and trust. We will not shy away from questioning long-standing concepts and paradigms, from scaling to voluntary tech accountability itself. 

The Forum will draw on the trajectory of Ranking Digital Rights (RDR), a tech transparency research program that renewed its mission in 2026 as an autonomous initiative after operating within larger institutional settings for 13 years. RDR’s reorientation toward community partnerships and localized accountability – and away from monolithic company assessments – will provide one of many templates we hope will emerge by the end of the session. We will also draw on the scholarly work of C. Thi Nguyen, whose research on the philosophy of games provides invaluable insight on how to avoid getting captured and devoured by the metrics and targets that CSOs often grapple with. 

The space we aim to create will be especially useful for “small but powerful” civil society groups that face significant resource constraints and seek ideas, partnerships, or creative adaptation strategies. Funders are welcome to follow along and take note of the shared stories and themes that emerge.

Structure
We will embrace a loose structure with four key checkpoints:

1. Small-group interactive reflection on existential challenges
2. Firestarter discussion
3. Small-group interactive reflection on strategies and structures of renewal
4. Rallying call

By the end of our time, we hope to have sown the seeds for new partnerships among participants and helped inspire structural strategies of resilience across many homes.

We'll delve into how communities globally are already reclaiming authority over their knowledge, data, and futures, and what rewilding intelligence might look like in practice; restoring consent, reciprocity, and collective governance to the systems that shape our lives. event.title: Rewilding AI: How Mother Tongue Digital Content Creation Shapes Just AI Futures
event.abstract:
Every major AI product, tool, or initiative in the world has one thing in common: it was designed primarily in English, overlooking millions of users who do not speak the language as their mother tongue or struggle to comprehend it. 

In January 2026, Navina Mutabazi decided to change that with a single Instagram Reel in Kiswahili, breaking down what artificial intelligence means for everyday Tanzanian life from her phone in Dar es Salaam. Within 24 hours the video had been watched by over 700,000 internet users, mainstream media was reposting it, and strangers were sharing it across community WhatsApp groups in Tanzania. The conversation jumped to TikTok and kept growing, and within a few days the series had crossed 500,000 internet users, not because an algorithm amplified it, but because a community had finally encountered AI in the language it thinks in, dreams in, and uses to raise its children. In the first part of this session,

In this session, Navina shares that journey openly: what she learned producing short-form AI content in Kiswahili from scratch, what worked, what surprised her, and what 700,000 views on Instagram taught her about language power and the politics of who gets to explain technology and to whom, drawing on her work advising UNICEF on data governance frameworks, leading the Sophia AI chatbot deployed across 25 countries, and training over 100 grassroots-led feminist organizations on ethical AI across Tanzania to make one central argument: mother tongue is not a workaround for excluded communities but the most powerful and most underestimated infrastructure for building genuine AI literacy. 

In the second part the session opens into a participatory forum where attendees from different countries and language communities bring their own contexts into the room, collectively exploring what community-owned, language-rooted technology education could look like at a global scale, one that grows naturally, spreads organically, and belongs to the communities that build it rather than the institutions that fund them.

event.title: Mycelia & Madness: Ecologies, Technology, & the Poetics of World-Building
event.abstract: This presentation explores writing techniques that subvert tropes of the science fiction genre, and examines how mental health and madness manifest in collective visions for a future where ecologies and technology are aligned. Sci-fi is a literary genre, but its world-building power can be applied in empowering ways; it is often the space where new technologies or their applications are imagined. The workshop employs poetic tools to engage in the practice of world-building to transform narratives around mental health as informed by our relationships to technology and the natural world. In doing so, the offering will illustrate how sci-fi emboldens communities to reorient visions of collective futures amid changing technologies and ecologies. The workshop engages in collective visioning that shift from reactionary futures towards deeper imaginings of what is (im)possible in a shifting world, with an orientation not merely towards preservation and protection, but towards development and transformation. Poetic and creative writing tools employed in science fiction and beyond will engage with such topics as identity, disability, and realtionality as informed by systems in the natural world -- such a mycelian networks, interstitial layers within bodies, the relationships between moss, trees, and lichen, and cosmic phenomenae such as dark matter. Likewise, we will look at the emergence of technology -- past, present, and future -- to inform the continued transformations of the above. The workshop will conclude by inviting the use of poetic and world-building tools in different environments to transcend paradigms, and direction on how to carry our collective visions of potential futures into the world(s) we have.

event.title: No Contract, No Cameras: A Procurement Power Lab
event.abstract:
For two decades, communities tried to govern surveillance technology through regulation: oversight ordinances, advisory boards, and transparency mandates. Vendors studied those rules, learning to engineer around them or use them to fuel runaway surveillance purchasing in US cities. Oakland has one of the strongest surveillance oversight laws in the country and still watched its City Council vote 7–1 to approve a $2.25 million contract expansion in December 2025. The oversight framework itself became the roadmap for circumvention.

Procurement Power is a different theory of change. It doesn't regulate surveillance; it refuses it outright. By treating contracting itself as a political act subject to democratic contestation, at least 30 U.S. localities used this approach to cancel or reject automated license plate reader (ALPR) contracts this past year.

This lab, developed by the Electronic Frontier Foundation and Local Progress, builds on learnings from direct engagement with over two dozen ALPR campaigns to model Procurement Power. Participants will start by working through the decision architectures of real case studies, Denver, Austin, Oakland, analyzing who held purchasing authority, what procedural moments were the actual chokepoints, and where campaigns had leverage to turn a vote against mass surveillance. They'll then develop campaign strategies for their own fights through a structured campaign clinic where they diagnose the specific obstacles and identify the most viable win conditions and termination pathways to end surveillance censors. 

The U.S. campaigns that anchor this session are the most documented examples available, but the pattern is not American. Surveillance vendors are expanding internationally, and procurement machinery in other countries is beginning to mirror the U.S. model, including cooperative purchasing equivalents, pilots, and vendor-drafted contract terms that authorize state surveillance and control. Facilitators will help translate U.S.-specific mechanics into equivalent structures for participants from other regions, and participants will leave with a range of tactics they can deploy to dismantle mass surveillance in their home contexts.

event.title: A Phenology of Data Centers: Reading Infrastructure as an Ecological Actor
event.abstract:
Phenology is the study of cyclic natural phenomena, telling our species when things bloom, migrate, emerge, and recede in relationship to the ecosystems they inhabit. A phenology of data centers transposes this practice onto our technological invasive species du jour, asking: when do these things draw the most water? When do they strain the regional grid? When do they arrive in communities, and what conditions preceded it? What does the neighborhood sound like when they do?


These questions require a different kind of attunement than power and water usage effectiveness can tell us, drawn out from timelapses of satellite imagery, water stress data, investigative journalism, community testimony, and deep listening. 


In this lab, participants build a phenological field guide to data center development from heterogenous evidence across multiple geographies. The session moves through 4 stages.
First, participants practice phenological thinking using something they already know - a houseplant, their favorite animal, a cool fungus - identifying what changes across seasons and what those changes reveal about the health of an ecosystem. 

Next, working in small groups, each with a packet of real source materials about a specific data center region (like satellite imagery, regional water stress data, and local journalism) groups identify what each source can tell them, what it cannot, and what they would need to know next.

Groups will then build a phenological timeline of their data center's life cycle, using a shared word bank: arrival, bloom, peak draw, dormancy, stress response, colonization, displacement, succession. For each term they use, they write one sentence of evidence. Where no evidence exists, the term becomes a question. Groups mark the moment where different source types tell conflicting or non-overlapping stories.

The lab closes with a gallery walk and a direct question: if a data center is an invasive species, what would a healthy ecosystem response look like, and who gets to decide?

The timelines participants build are the first draft of a collective field guide to data center phenology. They will be photographed, transcribed, and published as a free, downloadable zine after the festival.

The Majority World holds a myriad of alternatives that illustrate multiple ways AI technologies can support climate action through small, resource-efficient, community-centered climate solutions to pressing environmental challenges. From monitoring and data gathering, initiatives that involve environmental sensors or the translation and dissemination of information through chatbots to a wider range of intersections between AI tools and climate action and justice, including approaches that explore how communities can organize, reflect, and strengthen their agency beyond the roles of data collectors or data consumers. Examples of these technologies are fact-checking tools designed in multiple languages, including indigenous languages, that can help communities identify climate disinformation in contexts of crisis to tools developed for education, game development and speculative design that support young people in imagining climate-just futures.  

To support the re-imagination and re-direction of AI technologies, we at The Engine Room launched the AI for Climate Action, a year-long effort, centering Majority World leadership by mapping out their stories and collectively building a bottom-up framework to assess AI adoption.

  • The second one, will look to host dialogues to imagine how a future forest of many thriving wild alternative infrastructures herbs may look like, and what alliances and pathways can we delineate towards a transition for technology development that has justice, life, care and regeneration at the center.

event.title: The Milpa Network. A Tactile Audit of Representational Bias in AI
event.abstract:
Silicio & Flor is a community AI laboratory based in Ajalpan, Puebla, Mexico. We develop physical pedagogical tools enabling anyone to audit artificial intelligence systems. Our Mexico and Peru team brings this curriculum to Barcelona to expand and test it with the MozFest community.

The premise is tactile and straightforward. Standard computer vision models routinely fail analyzing the Mesoamerican milpa. Since their training data relies on industrialized monoculture, algorithms cannot process an ancient polyculture where corn, beans, and squash grow in mutualistic interdependence. To the processing logic of the machine, this systemic resilience registers as an error.

Through a four phase laboratory, we make this representational bias visible and correctable. First, we step away from screens. Using modeling compounds, tension wire, and organic seeds, working groups physically model the milpa as a three dimensional directed graph. We map biological mutualisms into mathematical weights, physically experiencing how imbalanced networks collapse.

Next, we transition this biological topology into computational logic. Using Semantic Rule Cards, participants encode Indigenous agricultural knowledge to actively correct an offline Vision Language Model in real time. We experience the exact moment community knowledge shifts from cultural narrative into technical input that rewires machine output.

No prior coding experience is required. Bring a willingness to rethink network architectures.

event.title: The Right to Kill Ideas
event.abstract:
Generative AI doesn’t fail through errors. It fails through accumulation—tone drifts, voices blur, identity erodes one acceptable output at a time. Nothing visibly breaks. Nobody notices until the voice is already gone.

This session is about the mechanism most AI systems don’t have: refusal.

I spent eighteen years building artist identities in the Romanian music industry. Then I started writing, and for the first time had to protect a voice that wasn’t built for someone else. I had no way to do it. So I built one: a governance system that evaluates every output against a defined identity and rejects what drifts. Independent validation across GPT, Claude, and Gemini reached 94% structural agreement, suggesting that identity can be evaluated consistently across frontier models.

Expect a direct case for treating refusal as a design principle rather than a limitation, grounded in a real forensic case study rather than theory. You’ll leave with a practical framework for measuring identity drift in generative systems—and a different question to ask of AI: not what it can produce, but what should be allowed to exist.

Built for anyone whose voice has to survive contact with a machine that never stops generating.

event.title: After the Moat: Open Source When Machines Don't Need Trust
event.abstract:
For decades, open source has won on a simple equation: code plus community plus trust. We know this from our first-hand experience as the stewards of scikit-learn, the global open standard for machine learning in Python, and others do, too. Permissive licenses (BSD-3-Clause, MIT, Apache 2.0) made the code freely available, brands and communities did the rest. AI is now testing every part of that equation.

The opening provocation: as AI commoditizes code, what's left of lasting value is brand, community, and trust. Non-permissive licenses get blunted when models can read the logic and rewrite it in any language under any license. That seemed to settle things in favor of permissive open source.

Then a second shift. Trust is a human need. It lowers suspicion and makes choices feel easy. Machines don't need it the same way. If they pick by popularity or frequency, the existing logic holds. But if AI can soon prove code correct against intent, or generate mathematically sound and optimally efficient code on demand, the trust argument starts to crack. Open source could lose much of its rationale, unless trust still anchors modular, composable systems and the humans who govern them.

This forum is a one-hour structured provocation. We open with the argument in roughly 15 minutes, including insights from scikit-learn, then break into facilitated groups around three questions:

  1. What does competitive advantage look like for an open source project when AI can rewrite its competitors on demand?
  2. Where does trust still anchor in modular, composable software: licensing, governance, provenance, human accountability?
  3. What does this mean for founders building alternatives to centralized, extractive platforms?

We close with a synthesis round and a short set of working hypotheses to take forward.

Who this is for: open source founders, principal engineers, license and governance people, AI safety folks, and anyone whose business model quietly assumes that code remains scarce or that trust remains a human-only category.

What people walk away with: a sharper map of where their moat actually sits in 2026 and beyond, three or four contested hypotheses to test against their own work, and a small group of people thinking about the same questions.

event.title: Small, Specialized, Sovereign: Helping Trustworthy AI Grow in the Wild
event.abstract:
The dominant story about AI in 2026 is that scale wins. Bigger models, more parameters, more centralized infrastructure, fewer providers. But there's a quieter story unfolding in the wild: specialized models — often orders of magnitude smaller, often fine-tuned by the organizations and communities that actually use them — are outperforming frontier LLMs on the tasks that matter in practice. And they're doing it while running on infrastructure their users control, with data that never leaves the building, at a fraction of the cost.

"Wilding" the AI stack is usually framed as a political or infrastructural question. We think it's also a question about trust: which models can we actually verify, instead of just being expected to believe? A 110M-parameter model that has been trained on your domain and knows when it doesn't know is more trustworthy than a trillion-parameter model that hallucinates fluently. The hyperscaler default tends to trade verifiability for convenience, sovereignty for ease, and calibrated uncertainty for overconfidence. For many of the tasks we actually need AI to do, such as classification, triage, decision support, and safety-critical workflows, that trade is often the wrong one.

We'll walk through concrete head-to-head benchmarks where small specialized models substantially outperform frontier LLMs on tasks like security vulnerability classification, consumer complaint routing, and semantic segmentation. They also provide meaningful advantages in cost, control, and deployability. We'll look at what makes the small-model approach work: domain-specific fine-tuning, calibrated uncertainty quantification so the model can refuse rather than hallucinate, and deployment on infrastructure the user controls. And we'll discuss the tooling, standards, and shared methodology that the ecosystem needs for this approach to flourish at the scale the moment demands.

The centralized frontier model isn't the only viable path, and in many cases it isn't even the best one. A wilder, more distributed, more verifiable AI ecosystem is already growing in parallel — and it deserves more attention, more tooling, and more deliberate cultivation. The session will close with discussion, where we'd like to surface where MozFest participants are already cultivating this ecosystem and what's most needed next.

event.title: Abolish AI vs. Build a People's AI: A Debate from Take Back Tech to MozFest
event.abstract:
Two teams. One room of organizers and technologists who do not agree on what to do about AI, and who are going to fight it out in front of you. Then, you'll enter the fray in small groups :) 

Team Abolish AI argues that the AI industry is extraction dressed as emancipation. It's the latest iteration of colonialism, powering rapid kill chains, mass surveillance, the detention and deportation system. Frontier systems demand centralized compute, dirty data centers, enclosed data, extractive labor, and tight state-corporate collusion, and they're all run by the broligarchs. There's no reform path, we need to abolish AI.

Team People's AI argues that yes, we do need to destroy or take over the Big Tech companies, but we can't let our imaginations be limited by them. The math underneath "AI" is a thousand-year human inheritance. The word "algorithm" comes from al-Khwārizmī, a 9th-century Persian scholar from what is now Iran. We are not surrendering that to Sam Altman, Peter Thiel, and Elon Musk. A People's AI is already being born at every layer of the stack: consented datasets, content moderator unions, public compute at libraries and universities, models like Switzerland's Apertus running on geothermal power, cooperatives like publicai.ch where 35,000 users and developers own their platform together. Our job is to seize the means of computation.

This session brings the movement debate that ran at Take Back Tech in Atlanta in April 2026 to MozFest. 

First, we model it. The facilitators (who were debate panelists at Take Back Tech) open with an abbreviated version of their arguments, then rebut each other. The crowd has paddles to hold up to indicate support or disagreement. 

After that, we'll break into small groups and every group will run its own debates, taking sides and pushing each other on the question.

We'll regroup at the end to compare notes, share anything that shifted, and surface new questions that came up.

You will leave with a clearer sense of where you stand, concrete examples of community-controlled tech that already exists, and a working format you can take home and run in your own community.

event.title: Snake Oil and Silver Bullets: What Privacy Tech Actually Works
event.abstract:
After nearly a decade working behind closed doors—as a senior advisor in the U.S. Senate—Christopher Soghoian returns to the public stage for a candid, unfiltered fireside chat on the state of consumer privacy technologies.

For years, the privacy market has promised that individual software choices can fix structural surveillance issues. This session strips away the marketing claims to evaluate what actually protects people, what creates a false sense of security, and what actively fails under scrutiny.

We will dig directly into three major consumer privacy battlegrounds:

  • VPNs: Marketing panacea vs. network reality. When do they shield users, and when do they simply re-route trust to an unvetted middleman?
  • Do Not Track & Global Privacy Control (GPC): Can browser-based preference signals hold up in a post-cookie web, or are they polite requests routinely ignored by bad actors?
  • Data Broker Opt-Out Services: Is automated deletion a viable long-term strategy, or a costly game of whack-a-mole that obfuscates a systemic policy failure?

Drawing on a career that bridges academic research, civil liberties advocacy, regulatory enforcement at the FTC, and legislative strategy in Congress, Soghoian offers an insider’s look at how policy and technical reality clash. Expect an honest, non-solicitation breakdown of where consumer tech stands—and where open-source, policy-backed standards must go next.

event.title: Community Design Principles Lab with Out in Tech
event.abstract:
Community Design Principles Lab with Out in Tech is a hands-on design lab, playtest, and co-creation opportunity for people who want to build more useful, welcoming, and sustainable communities.

Out in Tech will bring its beta Community Design Principles Kit and invite Mozilla Festival participants to help playtest and co-create it. The kit draws from Out in Tech’s decade-long experience building an 80,000-member volunteer-powered LGBTQ+ tech community, translating that experience into practical design principles that help shape how people are welcomed, connected, supported, and invited back.

The kit was built in response to seeing organic Out in Tech communities grow and falter on college campuses and in cities, then reach out to us for support. We wanted to design a fun and open system to test what we think we know and improve it. The Community Design Principles Kit is intended to be useful beyond any single identity, organization, or geography. We want to better understand what travels, what needs to be adapted, and what kinds of support help communities build on their own terms. Gatherwise.us has been a key design partner in helping us to identify and mobilize a community's unique collective skill set. 

The kit seeks to operationalize our core values — kindness, knowledge, belonging, and joy — into functional design principles.  These principles point community builders toward designing for human connection by asking practical questions: Can someone new, nervous, or alone enter easily? Do people leave with something they can use? Are we designing for an actual person and need? Where does connection actually happen? Why would someone return?

Participants do not need to prepare anything in advance. No prior facilitation, coding, or Out in Tech experience is required. They will choose from simple scenario cards or bring a real context from their own community, workplace, school, creative practice, organizing space, or local tech ecosystem. Working in small groups, they will use Out in Tech’s Community Launch Blueprint to design a first gathering, peer-learning experience, mentorship moment, community tool, or participation pathway — and consider whether that connection is best supported in person, virtually, or through a hybrid structure.

The lab will then stress-test each idea against a larger infrastructure question: What is the smallest set of supports needed to make this community experience repeatable, locally owned, and worth the effort?

This is not a presentation of a finished model. It is a live playtest. We want participants to use, adapt, challenge, and improve the kit based on their own contexts, needs, and lived experiences.

Together, we will explore community design as a practical skill: the ability to identify a real need, convene people, make learning usable, structure connection, prototype quickly, gather feedback, and build experiences people want to return to.

Participants will leave with a draft community experience, practical design prompts, and a clearer understanding of the infrastructure that helps inclusive tech communities become welcoming, useful, repeatable, and worth returning to.

event.title: Verifiable Agent Identity
event.abstract:
Autonomous AI agents are about to outnumber humans in every enterprise that takes AI seriously. The question of who an agent is, what  it's authorized to do, on whose authority, with what attribution is being decided right now, and the default answer is consolidating fast.

In most coding-agent deployments today, the agent operates with the developer's personal access token. The audit log says the developer did it. This works while agents run in supervised sessions on a developer's laptop with a human watching the terminal. It stops working the moment agents scale across many developers, many repos, many MCP tools, many CI jobs, or the moment tasks run long enough that the supervising human steps away.

When that breaks, the question of agent identity becomes urgent. The standards substrate for agent identity already exists, OAuth 2.0 token exchange and rich authorization, OpenID CIBA, SPIFFE workload identity, sender-constrained tokens via DPoP, the IETF WIMSE working group's emerging delegation semantics. Open-source implementations exist. The architectural decomposition that ties these into a coherent control plane: a Mission Authority, a Credential Broker, a Policy Decision Point, a Policy Enforcement Point, and an Evidence Chain, is publishable today and is the subject of our forthcoming paper Verifiable Agent Identity: Why Autonomous Agents Require a New IAM and Authorization Control Plane.

The question this session takes seriously is the one the track names directly: whether what's growing in the open becomes durable, or gets paved over. ZeroID, our open-source identity broker, ships clause-by-clause compliance suites against existing IETF RFCs plus OpenID CIBA and SPIFFE. Independent teams are building adjacent OSS in the same space. But durability is not guaranteed by existence: implementations that don't interoperate get isolated, standards-track participation without working code behind it loses to participation that has it, and maintainer attention that isn't sustained gets paved over.

This Developers Wilding session is a working conversation among the people who can keep the open path open: principal engineers, safety leads, OSS maintainers, founders, standards-track participants. The session opens with a fifteen-minute framing talk on the agent identity problem, the standards substrate, and the architectural decomposition that distinguishes the open path from the consolidation path. The remainder is a facilitated discussion around four questions:
1. What technical-architecture choices make open-source agent identity durable rather than brittle?
2. How do open implementations stay interoperable as hyperscaler patterns calcify?
3. Where should standards-track engineering effort be focused: which IETF drafts, which working-group seats, which spec gaps over the next twelve months?
4. What does it take for the products that exists today to still be operationally significant in three years?

We are running this at Highflame. ZeroID's design represents a series of architectural bets we have made in public, in code. Some will be vindicated by adoption; some will be wrong and need to be unwound. The session's premise is that the wider open ecosystem outpaces any single hyperscaler when engineers, maintainers, and standards folks coordinate on what matters technically rather than getting absorbed into their respective platforms.

Attendees leave with a concrete map of where agent identity is being defined and by whom, the technical primitives that compose into an accountable agent identity stack, a working OSS reference implementation, and a network of other engineers and maintainers in the same space. The wilder internet does not build itself. The engineers who hold the open path open are the ones who talk to each other about what is actually hard. This session is for that conversation.

event.title: A wild idea - from infrastructural power to abolition
event.abstract:
We view wilding as a prompt for a revolutionary reimagining of our organising, engagement with digital infrastructures, and our very existence. From inside a world of almost unchecked digital militarism and digitalisation proceeses that centralise and concentrate the power of large technology companies, many of us feel an impending sense of doom and hopelessness at how we get out os this.

 


Policy responses often feel futile, attempts at reform feel like bait for cooptation, and ‘alternatives’ often replicate existing power imbalances and a never ending cycle of extractivism, militarisation and exploitation in the digital economy.

 


And yet - truly radical takes on how to divest from the status quo are frequently sidelined as wild - unachievable, unrealistic and perhaps unimaginable. 

 


This session would invite participants into a conversation to reconsider what is a wild or radical within digital organising. Drawing from abolitionist organising frameworks and radical redistributive politics, we want to make space for wild conversations about where do we go next in digital organising. How do we challenge the tech-military complex? How do we reverse the infrastructural power of large technology companies over almost all aspects of collective life?  How should digital organising embrace abolitionism - of police, prisons, military and all the ways digital and carceral infrastructures collide? What would a redistributive politics look like, where public resources are not sucked into digital infrastructures and instead used for flourishing of collective life and our environments. 

 


Whilst we dont yet know the best format to do that, we imagine stating with some perspectives from a recent project interrogating how computational infrastructures around digital payment cards for asylum seekers can be understood and contested, with perspectives from migrant justice, abolition, digital identity and computational science. 

 

 

 

The Tech Infrastructure Coalition (TIC) explores how computational infrastructures (the cloud and end devices as their accessories) reconfigure and deplete collective life. In a world where digital extraction intersects with militarisation and securitsation, we work to articulate, contest and reimagine practice around digital technologies. event.title: Superhero Outfits for the Open and Agentic Web
event.abstract:
Firefox could be understood as one's "superhero outfit" for the Open Web - the clothing that gives you superpowers when it comes to privacy, security, memory, portability, and overal agency. Similarly, Thunderbird is the same kind of "superhero outfit" when engaging with the wild world of Email. Both of these tools work to ensure that neither the Web nor Email become a single-vendor consolidated vertical domain. This not only helps individuals express their agency over their digital lives, it also helps businesses (particularly startups!) avoid being locked-out of interesting opportunities.

But for this newly emerging Agentic Web, we may need a different kind of "superhero outfit" for us humans. We may need client-side, trustworthy tools that help us remember our conversations and results with different chatbots; monitor results for inaccuracies or bias; collaborate with other humans when engaging an AI model as a group; and to build and manage a fleet of agents who can be portable across foundation models and deployment platforms. With the Web and Email we had open standards (HTTP, HTML, SMTP, IMAP) that helped us define the boundaries between "client-side" (safe! us!) and "server-side" (the wildlands). Where are those boundaries when it comes to AI chatbots and agents? How will that evolve? 

In exploring this topic, the speakers will discuss a new tool from the creators of Thunderbird, called Thunderbolt, which addresses some of these issues. But we hope to engage the room on where they feel those boundaries lie - and what a new kind of "superhero outfit" for AI should look like.

event.abstract: Inclusion asks whose voices are in the room. Inheritance asks whose knowledge built the room. The technology industry has been answering the first question to avoid the second. This Talk is the second question. Eteroa Lafaele and Julia Pahina co-founded Fibre Fale AI, a Pacific-founded social enterprise operating from Aotearoa New Zealand. We reclaim AI to mean Ancestral Intelligence: the knowledge systems that existed before the Western technological architecture was built, and that were buried to make that architecture legible as universal.

Julia Pahina is CEO and Co-Founder of Fibre Fale AI, a Pacific-founded social enterprise operating from Aotearoa New Zealand. Her intellectual project is the politics of knowing in the AI age: who defines intelligence, what gets erased, and what becomes possible when we refuse the erasure.

The technology industry has spent a decade asking who is in the room. Julia asks whose knowledge built it. These are not the same question. Inclusion treats one knowledge system as default inheritance and every other as perspective brought in as a guest. The asymmetry is the problem, not the absence.

Fibre Fale AI reclaims AI to mean Ancestral Intelligence — the knowledge systems that existed before the Western technological architecture was built, and that were deliberately buried to make that architecture legible as universal. The Hibiscus Impact Model (HIM) is the methodology that makes this concrete: a Pacific-designed evaluation framework built from the Sāmoan proverb E so'o le fau i le fau — joining fibre to fibre, forming an unbreakable bond. Five outcomes. All independently assessed as Advancing.

Julia holds governance roles on the New Zealand Human Rights Commission Expert Advisory on AI, the World Economic Forum Global Futures Council on AI and Humanity, and the University of Auckland Council. She has worked with over 31,000 people in person and 11 million online. She is presenting at MozFest 2026 with co-founder Eteroa Lafaele.

Their work is anchored in their ancestral Arab heritage, while treating the oud as a living, iterative tradition. Clarissa’s sonic tapestry opens portals that nurture a sense of dignity and defiance to colonial erasure, be it in classrooms, on the streets in protests, or in intergenerational third spaces. Their 45-minute performance blends the rich traditions of Arabic music with contemporary composition and experimentation. Moving between intricate melodies, improvisation and moments of deep emotional intensity, Clarissa explores Palestinian heritage and the diasporic experiences of memory, longing and belonging.

event.title: Rewilding the Walled Gardens: Restoring Choice, Agency, and Competition Online
event.abstract:
Digital markets are often described as ecosystems. But many of today’s dominant digital ecosystems look less like open, living environments and more like walled gardens: carefully controlled spaces where defaults, prompts, rankings, switching barriers and interface choices determine what users see, choose and trust. This is increasingly true for emerging AI assistants and agents, which act as powerful new intermediaries that further entrench these walled gardens.

This session asks what it would mean to “rewild” these digital spaces and to move away from manipulative design and lock-in toward online environments where people can make meaningful choices, independent technologies can compete, and communities can shape the tools they rely on.

Harmful design practices, often described as dark patterns or deceptive design, are not limited to annoying cookie banners or subscription traps. They also appear at the system level. This happens when users are repeatedly nudged, when defaults are hard to change, when switching is made deliberately burdensome, or when operating systems and dominant platforms use their control over the user interface to privilege their own services.

Over time, these practices do more than frustrate individual users. They can entrench walled gardens, reinforce gatekeeper power, reduce the ability of people to choose alternatives, and make it harder for independent and community-oriented technologies to compete on the merits.

Drawing inspiration from Mozilla’s work on browser choice, digital competition, harmful design practices and user agency, the session will connect three issues that are too often discussed separately: user choice, consumer protection, and fair competition. It will explore: 

What does meaningful choice actually look like? 
When does design become manipulative? 
How have dominant platforms benefited from confusing, coercive or asymmetric interfaces? 
And how can communities, designers, researchers, policymakers and technologists push for digital environments that respect people’s decisions rather than trying to override them?
Participants will be invited to map examples of harmful design they encounter in everyday digital life, from default settings and consent flows to app stores, browser choice screens, operating systems, subscriptions and AI interfaces. Together, we will identify recurring patterns, discuss who benefits from them, and develop principles for user-respecting design that supports openness, competition and genuine agency.

The goal is to move beyond simply naming “dark patterns” and toward a shared understanding of how design can either concentrate power or redistribute it back to users and communities. In the spirit of MozFest’s Wilding theme, this session is about imagining digital spaces that are less controlled, less extractive and less closed — and more open, diverse, interoperable and alive.

event.title: Community networks as a methodology for building knowledge with quilombolas
event.abstract:
What if building communication infrastructure became a way of building knowledge, resilience, and community leadership? This interactive forum explores how community networks enable quilombola communities to learn by doing — designing, deploying, governing, and adapting connectivity solutions.

Drawing on more than 20 years of experience across Brazil, participants will discover how shared technical knowledge, intergenerational learning, and community governance strengthen territorial autonomy and ensure the long-term sustainability of local networks. We will discuss practical lessons from community networks implementation experiences and examine what learnings are leading us now to think about resilient infrastructure when climate disasters take place. 

In that sense, the session will also introduce the TRIDECS project, which investigates how different technologies infrastructures can strengthen preparedness and response to climate-related disasters. TRIDECS highlights how connectivity, local knowledge, and trusted communication systems become critical assets for resilience in vulnerable territories.

Join us to explore how community networks are not only connecting people, but also creating lasting knowledge, climate resilience, and pathways for communities to teach, adapt, and thrive together.

Leandro is vice-president of Pangea.org, and retired Professor of Computer Systems at the Universitat Politècnica de Catalunya (UPC), Barcelona, with over three decades of experience on the internet, digital systems, community networking, and sustainable digital infrastructures. A pioneer of the academic Internet in Spain in the late 1980s, he co-founded Pangea.org (1993) and the Internet Society Catalan Chapter (ISOC.Cat) in 1996 to extend Internet access to non-profits and the broader public. He speaks Catalan, Spanish, English and a bit of French.

He combines civil society activism and leadership with technical research, standards engagement, actively contributing to multistakeholder Internet governance processes at global and regional levels. He was Co-Chair of the IETF/IRTF GAIA (Global Access to the Internet for All) Working Group (2018-2022), fostering research and dialogue on technical and socio-economic approaches to meaningful connectivity. He also served as Co-Rapporteur of ITU-T Question 7/SG5 (2022-2024 period), contributing to standards on environmental sustainability, circular economy, and e-waste in ICT. Co-founded the eReuse.org initiative in 2015 for the reuse and traceability of ICT goods.

Leandro has been an active participant in the IGF, including involvement in Dynamic Coalitions such as DC3 (Community Connectivity) and the DC on Environment, promoting sustainable and community-driven digital infrastructures. He has held leadership roles within the Association for Progressive Communications (APC), including Chair of the Board (2017-), advancing rights-based and inclusive Internet policies. He is board member of NGOs: APC.org, Pangea.org, ISOC.CAT and AUCOOP.UPC.EDU.

His long-standing engagement with community networks, digital commons, open-source development, and cooperation-for-development initiatives —including projects connecting communities, hospitals, and schools in the Global South— provides grounded experience linking technical design, governance, and social impact.

event.title: A Strategic Outlook for Digital Commons: Technology, Communities, and Governance
event.abstract:
Digital Commons are shared digital infrastructure that is collectively built and governed, and they are having a moment in European policy, albeit an ambiguous one. Sovereignty rhetoric is creating new openings for commons-based approaches to organising around, governing, and investing in public digital infrastructure that works for a plurality of Member States. This is partly what is proposed via ongoing initiatives like the Digital Commons EDIC and the Open Internet Stack. That said, the European Commission risks absorbing them while adopting largely statist, protectionist, or purely industrial framings that hollow out their meaning.

This talk navigates that tension directly, drawing on research from the NGI Commons project to offer a clear-eyed account of where things stand and what communities, researchers, and advocates can do about it. The talk will begin by mapping what Digital Commons are with sovereignty with precision: what each means, how they relate, and why distinctions in types of commons matter. From there, the talk examines the current EU policy moment and the role of Digital Commons in it: the sovereignty turn, the competitiveness and industrial policy logic n, the AI race framing, and what these shifts mean for the EU’s broader policy ambitions.

event.title: AI is the Next Global Plantation: Unless we Build Indigenous Data Sovereignty
event.abstract:
Overview
This talk will compare the buildout of AI and AI companies, to the global plantation industry of the 18th and 19th centuries that ravaged colonized states around the world. It will also offer solutions and invite discussions around how Indigenous Data Sovereignty, ancestral knowledge, and modern systems engineering can build a more equitable, just, and humanity-serving model, instead of the extraordinarily extractive empire-building model. 
The talk will describe how we can build Indigenous tech and data governance on our own terms — from Hawaii and Mauritius to Turtle Island, Chad, and Pakistan, rooted in self-determination. The talk will be co-presented by two Native Hawaiian (indigenous) leaders in the Indigenous Data Sovereignty movement: Dr. Keolu Fox (UCSD) and Dr. Josiah Hester (Georgia Tech). Additionally, we hope to include AfrotroniX, a musician and afrofuturist from Chad, who Dr. Hester co-presented with at Rhizome 7x7.
Format
The talk is meant as a lively, sometimes comedic provocation that shares dystopian, utopian, and realistic scenarios for the Global AI Plantation, and ends with provocative examples from around the world on how Indigenous people and global south communities are re-creating and reimagining AI. Participants in the session will be invited to vote in real time and share feedback using slid.o and other mechanisms, to ensure interaction through the delivery. After the talk, participants will be invited to form breakout groups and work together on a fast paced prompt of "re-imagining and rewilding AI systems from Indigenous perspectives." If possible, tables will be asked to share out briefly, if not possible, tables will be able to log final ideas and titles of work, and collectively vote on the best or most promising directions.
The outcome of the talk / breakout groups will be synthesized into a short report and shared back with attendees, as well as presented at the US Indigenous Data Sovereignty Conference in April 2027. 
Hawaii Context and Comparison
Dr.s Fox and Hester, both Indigeonus Native Hawaiian scienutst, will tell the story of the talk via lived and ancestral experience, while also drawing on their expertise in computing systems.
On Jan. 17, 1893, the Hawaiian Kingdom was overthrown by a group made up largely of sugar planters.
The legacy of plantation agriculture is still visible across Hawaiʻi in diverted water, depleted soils, food import dependency and an economy structured around extraction. A place once rich in water, life and culture, that sustained a million people, had its waiwai (wealth) redirected into producing sugar and pineapple that enriched the “Big Five.”
Plantations reorganized the entire ecosystem of Hawaiʻi to serve distant markets, concentrating land and water under a few owners while exporting wealth off-island. The result was ecological simplification, cultural disruption and long-term dependency. Today, the commodity is no longer sugar or pineapple or sandalwood. It is machine intelligence — computer, data and the infrastructure that powers them. 
Just as the plantation industry ravaged Hawaiʻi (and so many other places around the world), exporting and extracting innumerable resources, the profit of which built the modern inequitable system, so to is AI (led by Big Tech companies) going down this same path. 
Long before plantations, Hawaiʻi sustained a large population through a sophisticated system of land and resource management known as the ahupuaʻa: a division of land from mauka to makai that integrated forests, agriculture, freshwater, and fisheries into a self-sustaining whole. Resources were managed locally, with deep knowledge of place and an ethic of stewardship that maintained abundance over generations.
What would it mean to design our islands’ computing infrastructure with those principles in mind? What would it mean if we, Kānaka Maoli and Kamaʻāina, were the leaders in ensuring the AI data centers that inevitably do arrive on our lands were built differently?
The talk will specifically approach data centers, AI, and sovereignty, from this Indigenous perspective, and invite participation from the audience.

Keolu Fox is a Kanaka ʻŌiwi and associate professor at the University of California, San Diego, affiliated with the Department of Anthropology, the Global Health Program, the Halıcıoğlu Data Science Institute, the Climate Action Lab, and the Indigenous Futures Institute.
